CM Afridi slams Governor Kundi for 'unconstitutional' meetings, claims move intended to provoke KP govt. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi on Wednesday slammed Governor Faisal Karim Kundi for holding “unconstitutional” meetings, contending that the move was an “attack on democracy”.

His remarks came a day after Governor Kundi chaired a meeting with the KP chief secretary and inspector general (IG) on the province’s security situation.

Addressing the 60th cabinet meeting in Peshawar, Afridi said that the KP governor, who belonged to the PPP, staged a “drama” yesterday by summoning the meeting and termed the move “unconstitutional”.

“The governor convening such a meeting in the presence of a provincial government with a two-thirds majority is unacceptable,” he said.

“The provincial assembly, cabinet and government are fully functional and intact,” the PTI leader asserted, terming Kundi’s act an “attack on the Constitution and democracy”.

Afridi contended that the purpose of the governor’s “unconstitutional activities” was to “provoke the provincial government and force it to react”.

However, he advised PTI workers to stay peaceful and abide by the law and the Constitution.

Calling on the province’s chief secretary and IG, the chief minister urged them not to comply with any unconstitutional or illegal order from anyone if he does not order them to do so.

He reiterated that KP’s people and administration had made “countless sacrifices” in the fight against terrorism.

“If someone pushes you to follow any unconstitutional order, do not follow it. It can damage our province or the country.”

He also called on the chief secretary to urge the provincial administration not to indulge in any unconstitutional activity and to take action against those who were accused of corrupt practices.

The chief minister then took aim at Kundi’s PPP, blaming ex-president Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, along with General Yahya Khan, for the separation of East Pakistan, now Bangladesh.

He accused President Asif Ali Zardari of “intending to make another East Pakistan here“.

“We will not allow any conspiracy to break up Pakistan to succeed,” he asserted.

“The party that raised the slogan of democracy separated Bangladesh from Pakistan in the past for its personal interests,” he alleged.

“Prioritising personal interests over national interests has been the PPP’s practice,” he further claimed.

Afridi’s remarks come amid heightened tensions between the Centre and the PTI-led opposition, with the latter going ahead with its long march despite warnings from the Centre of action against any such move.

Hours-long talks over the weekend between a joint delegation of the government and PPP, and the opposition alliance ended in a deadlock, with both sides blaming the other for the breakdown.

Political temperatures have also remained high due to speculations of the Centre imposing governor’s rule in the province, with Kundi and Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi discussing the move on Sunday.

‘Policy shift is necessary’

The KP CM also reiterated his objection to the Centre’s counterterrorism policy and defended his government’s efforts in supporting the police in the fight against terrorism.

He contended that terrorism had been “imposed on the province again”, asserting that the PTI-led provincial government had always supported the police and the people of KP.

Afridi maintained that he had been making efforts to strengthen the police, the Counter-Terrorism Department and Special Branch since he took the oath on Oct 15, 2025.

“The KP police have the most modern weapons and equipment compared with any other police force in Pakistan,” the chief minister said.

He contended that the federal government had always treated KP like a “stepchild”.

“The tribal districts were merged into KP in 2018, but they have not been fully integrated financially to this day,” CM Afridi claimed, adding that the financial rights of the tribal districts agreed upon at the time of their merger had not been provided yet.

The PTI leader went on to claim that federal governments had “continuously imposed military operations” on KP since 2004.

“People displaced by the federal government’s wrong policies kept crying on the streets, but they have still not received full compensation,” he said, adding that nearly Rs100 billion in compensation were still outstanding.

“Those whose homes were destroyed, families affected and mosques demolished are still wandering from pillar to post for their compensation.”

He highlighted that while a compensation of only Rs400,000 per household had been fixed for tribal families, they had not even been paid the promised amount.

Afridi stressed that a commitment was also made to provide between Rs370million and Rs380m per month to displaced people from North Waziristan at the Baka Khel camp. “The displaced people of Baka Khel are still not being provided the monthly amount as promised.”

“It is the provincial government’s responsibility to stand with people displaced by the federal government’s wrong policies,” the chief minister stated, adding that his government had provided Rs21bn for displaced people.

“The provincial government also has to bear responsibility for losses caused by military operations and collateral damage as a result of drone attacks,” Afridi said.

He also remarked that the individuals making decisions in the federal government had no sense of the difficulties faced by the people as a result of those decisions.

“If the federal government is sincere with KP, it should upgrade the province’s NFC (National Finance Commission) share and pay its outstanding dues of around Rs125bn to the province that has sacrificed 80,000 precious lives,” he demanded.

Afridi reaffirmed that KP had to fight terrorism as well as deal with the situation created by the federal government’s policies.

“The KP government and police are serious about maintaining law and order. Turning the police into personal servants and assigning them other tasks is wrong,” he declared.

“If the policy of KP’s stakeholders is followed, peace can be established within 100 days,” the PTI leader insisted.

He questioned why peace could not be established in the province “despite 14,000 intelligence-based operations and 22 major military operations over 22 years”, terming it a “failure of the federal policy”.

Afridi maintained that if the issue of peace still exists in KP even after 22 years, the federal government should change its policy against terrorism if it was “serious in doing so”.

“The excuse that KP is not cooperating is unacceptable; the same policy is also failing in Balochistan,” he claimed, as both provinces have witnessed an increase in terrorist activities in recent years.

“The Balochistan government is cooperating with the federal government, but peace has still not been established there,” Afridi said, claiming the Centre’s counterterrorism policy was neither effective in KP nor in Balochistan.

“A shift in policy is necessary. KP can establish peace within 100 days,” he reaffirmed.

In his address, Afridi also once again criticised Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz’s remarks that her province faced no threats from India, despite the state’s narrative of the presence of Indian proxies in Pakistan in the face of Fitna al Hindustan.

Asif says ‘enough is enough’

Meanwhile, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif assailed the PTI-led KP government for continuing its “complete detachment from terrorism in the province and criminal indifference”.

“Enough is enough!!!” he wrote in a post on X.

“The PTI provincial government is roaming the streets for a so-called failed political long march, while its facilitators have unleashed a fresh wave of terrorism against the people of KP during this very time,” he said.

The minister recalled Tuesday’s attacks in Dera Ismail Khan, where customs officials were among five people killed.

He remarked that the entire provincial cabinet, including the chief minister, was “numb to this serious matter and fully engrossed in their politically failed long march”.

“As always, these insensitive and shameless people did not even condemn the innocent murder of these five individuals in DI Khan, offered no condolences to the grieving families, did not attend their funerals or, at the very least, visit their homes to express regret,” Asif regretted.

“This is inexcusable by any standard.”

Instead, the defence minister noted, the KP CM had scheduled a meeting today at his party’s behest to reprimand the IG and chief secretary for attending the governor’s security meeting.

“The chief minister and his cabinet of a province under the scourge of terrorism have completely abandoned the province’s people to the mercy of the terrorists. That is why the people of KP are protesting against the provincial government on the streets in various areas.

“This can no longer be tolerated,” Asif declared.

The defence minister accused the KP government of being in “complete collusion” with terrorists, saying there was evidence available of “its facilitator ecosystem, which every Pakistani has witnessed with their own eyes over the past three years”.

Recalling past arrests of ex-premier Nawaz Sharif and his family members, as well as PML-N leaders, Asif asserted: “Time has proven that the allegations were just allegations and they were imprisoned on Imran Khan’s behest.”

Yet, he stressed, the PML-N fulfilled its parliamentary role responsibly under the Constitution and did not hold the country and institutions “hostage”.

“It fought a legal and constitutional battle in the courts and parliament. It did not ally with the Taliban,” Asif declared.

The defence minister said that the “time has come to make crucial decisions”.

“KP cannot be left any longer to the mercy of incompetent, insensitive rulers and Taliban allies,” he avowed.

Asif further stressed that the unity of the country cannot be put at risk. “An entire province cannot be held hostage. Enough is enough.”

item.title: Australia prepare for first test in South Africa since'Sandpapergate'. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Australia play their first test in South Africa since the 2018 ball-tampering scandal when they start a three-match series in Durban on Friday, with the visitors unlikely to face more than a few heckles over the incident that rocked the sport eight years ago.

The tourists efforts to roughen up the ball using sandpaper, and aid reverse swing, in Cape Town in March 2018 were caught on camera and led to a major reckoning for the game in Australia, with captain Steve Smith among those banned for their role in the subterfuge.

South Africa have played tests in Australia since Sandpapergate, and Australia have toured South Africa in the interim for limited-overs internationals.

The scandal has attracted little media focus in South Africa over recent weeks in comparison to the attention devoted to the incident in the Australian press.

After dethroning Australia last year in a thrilling World Test Championship final at Lords to win a first major title, South Africa are focused on improving their chances of a return to the final at the end of the 202527 WTC cycle.

Australia are also in need of a boost after a surprise home test defeat by Bangladesh in August and with an Ashes tour to England starting next June.

The pitch at Kingsmead often proves a fickle track but should offer the spinners a chance to play a leading role in a change from South Africas usually seamer-friendly surfaces.

It is unusual for South Africas chances to be largely entrusted to their spin attack, but Simon Harmer and Keshav Maharaj wreaked havoc in India last November when they triumphed in their last two test outings.

Spin was also a key factor for the home side as they beat Australia in the recent One-Day International series.

South Africa may therefore opt to rest frontline attack bowler Kagiso Rabada from the test as he continues his comeback from a hamstring injury.

Injury to Australia all-rounder Cameron Green opens up a chance at number five for Cooper Connolly, or a fairytale return for 34-year-old Nic Maddinson after recovering from cancer.

South Africas also has a choice to make over their number three batsman, with coach Shukri Conrad having several options including a potential first cap for 30-year-old Marques Ackerman.

item.title: Guardians of the cage. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
It was a cold, crisp, snowy day in February 1966 when in a New York City studio, a masterpiece of a song, "It's a Man's Man's Man's World" was co-written by James Brown and Betty Jean Newsome.
James Brown, who was then at the absolute peak of his commercial popularity, performed this song in live shows for the rest of his musical career.
The song starts with "This is a man's world" and goes on to aggressively ascribe all the works of the modern civilization such as cars, trains, boats, and electric light solely to male efforts; however, as if to pour oil on troubled waters, the song ends with a casual claim that it all would mean "Nothin' without a woman or a girl."
Interestingly, while Brown globally popularized the phrase "This is a man's world" through his "biblically chauvinistic" track, Newsome later claimed to have written the lyrics based on her own observations of gender dynamics.
Do you see the irony? This historic anthem that was profoundly criticized for its extreme machismo was given its meaning by Newsome, a woman herself, who fought for decades so her name was not erased from its history.
Sixty years ago, a phrase became universal due to the lyrical genius of a woman; the same phrase is still being used by our male-dominated society whenever patriarchy demands our women to be put in their “rightful” position.
In 1990, Sylvia Walby defined patriarchy as “a system of social structures and practices in which men dominate, oppress, and exploit women.” In other words, patriarchy is a system that predominantly favours men.
Yet, are men the only ones to forge ahead with patriarchy? Has it ever crossed your mind how women themselves, wearing the invisible cloak of patriarchy, have been perpetuating the faults of the system in the name of tradition all this time?
One bewildering characteristic of patriarchy is that it pits women against women. Each time a mother, a female teacher, a mother-in-law, a female friend, points the policing fingers at the woman next to her for not yielding to the system, the chain of patriarchy moves forward.
It is a common experience of girls growing up in Bangladesh to face judgement from women. The mechanism of patriarchy is so deeply rooted into our society that many women preach oppression instead of being a part of the sisterhood.
Remember the legendary cartoon Meena ? In this timeless children’s show, Meena’s mother and grandmother, clearly biased towards her brother Raju, would often discriminate between the siblings. Sadly, most girls born and growing up with brothers in Bangladeshi households are no stranger to this discrimination.
Unfortunately, the very first whip of patriarchy almost always comes from the mothers, who are often found policing their daughters’ bodies and behaviours so that the daughters conform to the entrenched norms of this patriarchal society.
Mothers often teach their daughters to adjust, to endure, to follow the rules, while their sons grow up knowing the world will negotiate the rules for them.
One survey showed that 93% families in Bangladesh see their sons as a blessing, while 96% see their daughters as a “problem” to the family and the country. The discrimination is reflected in dietary portions, permission to play outside, and the freedom to make friends.
This motherly discrimination is topped with the unwanted surveillance of the “aunty society.” The women from the neighbourhood or the mothers waiting outside schools and coaching centres almost invariably engage in tracking down girls for having male friends, talking or laughing too loud, dressing up, or wearing light makeup. These small acts of freedom often end up becoming the gravest of sins.
For many girls, even classrooms become a place for moral policing. Female teachers, who should be providing a safe outlet for the students, justify their humiliating remarks as “protection.” Moreover, in many co-ed institutions, female teachers sometimes show unfair preferences towards male students.
Among peers, women frequently face criticism disguised as opinions from other women, based on their life choices, work positions, or clothing.
Women who conform to societal expectations often feel superior and disdain women who choose to live lives that don’t align with those beliefs. Conformity thus turns into a currency for winning in life for women embodying patriarchy.
This submission to patriarchy continues as a mother-in-law’s abuse of her daughter-in-law activates the cycle of unjust treatment and passes it down from one generation to the next. As the mother of the groom, her actions of looking down on the bride's family and demanding dowry eventually turn into violence against the daughter-in-law.
And when the violent treatment compels the daughter-in-law to return to her parents’ house, it is often her mother who sends her back to her in-law’s house in the name of family honor. To these mothers, a dead daughter is far better than a divorced daughter.
So, should we consider these women culpable for the continuity of patriarchy? Before answering this question, we should ask a more important one: Why do women partake in this vile practice?
Denied direct power, as argued by author and academic Deniz Kandiyoti, many women learn to negotiate security by adapting to the system’s rules rather than resisting. Women submit to patriarchy as a survival mechanism and to gain authority over other women.
However, the consequences of this chain of patriarchy teach women to be each other’s judges instead of allies. It pierces through the sisterhood and hides structural patriarchy behind a facade of women blaming each other. Meanwhile, the system itself is perpetuated through whoever is closest to it.
To break through the shackles of patriarchy, women need to recognize the contradictions that make them the silent flag-bearers. Decoding the patterns can easily turn the contention into cohesion. This is why, when sisterhood refuses to become patriarchy’s ally, it motivates women to heal and grow together.
Nadia Afroze Disha is a lecturer at Brac Business School, Brac University. Purnasha Aurora is a student of Economics at Brac University.

item.title: Private universities are challenging old academic hierarchies. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The latest Times Higher Education rankings offer Bangladesh’s private universities something more valuable than a place on an international table: They offer evidence that the country’s higher education landscape is changing.
The change is not simply about private universities moving upward while public universities move downward. It is about a new competition emerging in Bangladeshi higher education, where institutional ambition, research capacity, international engagement, and responsiveness to changing academic expectations increasingly determine visibility.
For years, the conventional hierarchy of Bangladeshi universities seemed almost unquestionable. Public universities, particularly the older ones, occupied the symbolic high ground. Their historical importance, academic traditions, alumni networks and contributions to national life gave them an authority that newer institutions could not easily challenge.
Private universities were often regarded as commercially driven alternatives, useful for students who could not enter the public system or preferred a different academic environment. That perception is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain.
The Times Higher Education World University Rankings 2027 provide an important indication of why. Of the four Bangladeshi universities placed in the 801 to 1000 band, three are private: American International University-Bangladesh, Daffodil International University, and North South University. Jahangirnagar University is the only public university in that group.
This does not mean that private universities have suddenly become superior to public universities in every respect. Rankings cannot settle such a complicated question. But they do tell us something important: Several private institutions have developed measurable strengths that allow them to compete with universities carrying decades of institutional history.
That development deserves neither exaggerated celebration nor instinctive suspicion. It deserves serious examination.
One reason private universities have been able to advance is that many of them were born into a different academic environment. They did not inherit the enormous weight of tradition that older public universities carry. They had to build their reputations almost from scratch.
That created pressure to establish recognisable academic brands, attract qualified faculty, develop modern infrastructure, maintain relationships with industry and present themselves as internationally-oriented institutions. In an increasingly competitive higher education market, standing still has consequences.
The same shift is visible beyond conventional university rankings. IUBAT, for instance, has built a notable record in sustainability and environmental performance, ranking 1st in Bangladesh, 113th in Asia, and 197th globally in the 2026 UI GreenMetric World University Rankings among 2016 universities from 110 countries.
Such achievements are particularly noteworthy because sustainability remains an area where many of Bangladesh's public universities have yet to establish comparable international visibility. The point is not that private universities have solved the problem, but that some are showing how institutional commitment can turn sustainability from a ceremonial slogan into measurable practice.
There is also a generational difference in institutional thinking. Many private universities were established when globalization, digital technology, and international academic mobility were already becoming central to higher education.
Their institutional cultures therefore developed around a world in which universities were expected to communicate internationally, collaborate across borders, engage with employers, and demonstrate measurable academic performance.
For institutions seeking students in a competitive market, international recognition is not merely a matter of prestige. It is part of the product they are offering.
This is where the ranking story becomes more interesting. Times Higher Education does not assess universities simply by asking how famous they are. Its indicators consider teaching, research environment, research quality, industry engagement and international outlook.
A university therefore cannot rely indefinitely on its historical reputation. Reputation may open a door, but research output, academic infrastructure and international engagement increasingly determine whether the door remains open.
The performance of private universities should consequently be understood as a challenge to complacency across the entire sector. If a relatively young institution can enter the same ranking band as universities with much longer histories, the question is not only what the younger institution is doing right. The more uncomfortable question is what established institutions may be doing too slowly.
This does not make the rankings an unquestionable measure of educational quality. University rankings have limitations. They favour institutions with strong research systems, international networks, reliable data and the capacity to participate effectively in global evaluation mechanisms.
A university's social contribution, teaching culture, affordability, accessibility and influence on national intellectual life cannot always be reduced to a numerical position or ranking band. Nor should a university become obsessed with improving its ranking at the expense of educating students.
Yet dismissing rankings altogether would be equally unwise. International rankings may be imperfect, but they provide benchmarks that universities can use to identify institutional weaknesses.
They force universities to ask difficult questions about research productivity, citation impact, doctoral programmes, international collaboration, industry connections and academic governance. These are not meaningless concerns.
Perhaps the most important lesson from the latest ranking is therefore not that private universities are defeating public universities. It is that the old public-private divide is becoming less useful for understanding academic performance.
A university should be judged increasingly by what it produces, how it teaches, how it researches, how it engages with society and how effectively it prepares students for a changing world.
There is another issue that deserves attention. Some universities participated in the ranking but did not receive a final numerical position because they had not met the necessary conditions.
They were instead placed in the "reporter" category. This is significant because participation itself indicates that institutions are becoming conscious of the importance of international benchmarking. But participation should be the beginning, not the achievement.
The real challenge is to build the academic systems required to move from reporting data to demonstrating sustained performance.
For private universities, the latest results should bring confidence, but also caution. Ranking success can easily become a marketing slogan. A university that enters an international ranking today can fall out tomorrow if its research culture stagnates.
Sustainable academic reputation cannot be built through advertising campaigns, impressive buildings or expensive programs alone. It requires serious faculty recruitment, academic freedom, research funding, ethical governance, strong libraries and laboratories, rigorous assessment, and an environment in which teachers are encouraged to produce knowledge rather than merely deliver courses.
Public universities face a different but equally important challenge. Their historical advantages remain substantial, but history cannot function as an automatic ranking mechanism.
Public universities possess enormous intellectual resources and some of the country's finest scholars. What they need is an institutional environment capable of converting those resources into stronger research, better international collaboration, and more consistent academic output.
The real winner, if the trend continues, could be Bangladeshi higher education itself. Competition can force institutions to improve. A student should not have to choose between the prestige of an old university and the modernity of a new one. Ideally, every university should be compelled to offer both intellectual depth and contemporary academic opportunities.
The rise of private universities should therefore not be viewed as the decline of public universities. It should be viewed as a warning against the idea that reputation is inherited permanently.
Universities, like ideas, must continually prove their relevance. Bangladesh's higher education system will advance when institutions stop asking who traditionally occupied the top and start asking who is doing the work required to deserve it.
HM Nazmul Alam is an academic, journalist, and political analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently he teaches at IUBAT.

item.title: Our failure to contain dengue. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The grim toll of Bangladesh’s ongoing dengue crisis continues to rise, exposing a chronic failure of public health management and municipal governance.
With the national death toll climbing past 280 as of October 6, daily hospitalizations nearing 2,000, and a sharp spike in infections hitting regional hubs like Chittagong, what should be a manageable seasonal illness has once again transformed into a deadly public health emergency.
That September registered as the deadliest month of the year proves that official interventions remain woefully inadequate, reactive, and out of step with reality.
The current surge also highlights a persistent breakdown in vector control and local administration oversight. Across Dhaka, Chittagong, and rural districts, residents routinely report invisible city corporation workers, irregular fogging drives, and unmonitored stagnant water at construction sites and public spaces.
While municipal authorities predictably shift blame onto public carelessness, the reality from finger pointing is more suffering and death - an outcome nobody wants in the country.
As such, we need an administrative apparatus that does not act only after hospital wards overflow. Spraying ineffective larvicides or launching sporadic "crash programs" after the peak transmission season takes hold is an exercise in public relations, not public health.
Simultaneously, we do need more public awareness and recognition that mosquitoes must be stopped from breeding.
Ultimately, as has been stated numerous times, dengue has long moved on from being an unexpected annual surprise. It is, and has been for some time now, an endemic threat that requires year-round, science-driven mitigation.
We need our health authorities across the country to abandon their seasonal complacency. Treating human lives as acceptable collateral in what has become an annual administrative failure is unacceptable. We must act with the urgency needed to halt this preventable devastation.

item.title: Lethal force is not the answer. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The latest incident of firing by the Indian Border Security Force (BSF), which left two Indian nationals critically injured, serves as another grim reminder of a persistent, unacceptable crisis along the Bangladesh-India frontier.
This recent shooting underscores a broader, fundamental reality: The routine resort to lethal force by Indian border guards is a systemic issue that threatens human lives and undermines regional stability, regardless of the victims' nationality.
That reports also suggest that the BSF personnel detained them and tried to push them into Bangladesh, and fired after they resisted, is also deeply concerning, and needs clarification and investigation into the matter.
For years, high-level diplomatic meetings and ministerial summits between Dhaka and New Delhi have concluded with repeated assurances that non-lethal weapons would be prioritized and border fatalities brought down to zero.
Yet, on the ground, it is safe to say that trigger-happy responses remain far too frequent for comfort.
Tragic incidents involving firearm usage along an international border, often over petty smuggling or unauthorized crossings, defy basic international law enforcement standards. Surely we can agree that lethal force must strictly be a measure of last resort against imminent threats to life.
This cycle of violence cannot be normalized and must be condemned by all. Border management between two neighbouring nations, that too with such deep economic and diplomatic ties, requires more restraint and operational discipline.
It is high time to move past platitudes and enforce strict accountability. BSF personnel who violate non-lethal mandates must face thorough, independent investigations and clear legal consequences.
Resorting to live ammunition against unarmed or fleeing individuals breeds public resentment, fuels cross-border tension, and ultimately undermines the spirit of bilateral cooperation. We expect better.

item.title: A roof is not enough. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
A family finds a cheaper home on the outskirts of Dhaka. On paper, it looks affordable. But the father now spends hours commuting to work and a sizeable share of his income on transport. The children have little space to study. Waterlogging makes the neighborhood difficult to access during heavy rain. And every rent increase forces the family to reconsider what to cut from the monthly budget: food, healthcare, education, or savings.
So, is this really affordable housing?
This is the question we need to ask as we observe World Habitat Day and reflect on the call for “Adequate Housing for All.” Housing is too often discussed in terms of buildings: how many apartments have been constructed, how many plots have been developed, or how many families own their homes. But adequate housing is not simply four walls and a roof. It is about whether a home allows people to live safely, affordably, and with dignity and whether its location enables them to participate in the city.
For Bangladesh, this distinction is increasingly important. The 2022 Population and Housing Census shows that while about 80.8 percent of households nationally lived in their own dwellings, the figure was only 55.6 percent in urban areas. Around 34.7 percent of urban households were renters who did not own another dwelling elsewhere.
The more recent picture suggests that rental dependence remains significant. According to reporting based on Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics data, around 45 percent of households in Dhaka Division were renting or subletting their dwellings in 2023, compared with about 19 percent nationally. At the same time, the House Rent Index has continued to rise; BBS data show a 5.19 percent year-on-year increase in the July-September 2025 quarter, followed by 5.24 percent in October-December 2025.
These figures make the issue very tangible. For a large share of urban Bangladesh, housing is not an ownership question; it is a rental question. Homeownership therefore cannot be the only measure of housing success. For millions of Bangladeshis, particularly migrants, young workers, students, newly formed households, and low- and middle-income families, rental housing is not a temporary arrangement on the way to ownership. Rental housing is their housing.
Yet our housing discourse continues to focus heavily on land ownership, apartment ownership and new construction. Rental housing deserves far greater policy attention. We need better rental-market data, greater tenure security, transparent mechanisms for rent adjustment and incentives to expand affordable rental housing in well-connected locations.
This brings us to perhaps the most overlooked dimension of housing affordability: location.
A Tk10,000 home close to employment, public transport, schools and healthcare may ultimately be more affordable than a Tk7,000 home that requires several hours and substantial transport expenditure every day. Housing costs therefore cannot be understood separately from mobility costs. We need to start asking not simply, “How much does this house cost?” but, “How much does it cost this household to live here?”
Housing also has consequences that extend far beyond urban planning. Housing policy is education policy, health policy and, increasingly, climate policy. Consider a child living in an overcrowded home without adequate lighting, ventilation or a quiet place to study. Improving the school alone cannot remove all the disadvantages that child experiences. Housing conditions influence sleep, health, concentration and learning opportunities. Excessive rent can also leave families with less money for education, nutrition and healthcare.
Climate change adds another layer of urgency. In Bangladesh, flooding, waterlogging, cyclones, river erosion, salinity and extreme heat already affect where and how people live. A dwelling cannot be called adequate if it is affordable today but repeatedly flooded tomorrow, or if poor ventilation makes it dangerously uncomfortable during extreme heat.
Climate-resilient housing therefore requires more than stronger buildings. It requires risk-sensitive land-use planning, protection of wetlands and floodplains, better drainage, heat-sensitive design, energy efficiency, resilient infrastructure and community-based adaptation.
But resilience should not become an excuse for displacement. This is particularly relevant to informal settlements and historic neighborhoods such as Puran Dhaka. Demolishing older housing and replacing it with expensive apartments may improve physical building quality while making the neighborhood unaffordable to its original residents. The result can be better buildings but less inclusive cities.
Where feasible, upgrading existing communities should therefore come before displacement-oriented redevelopment. Better sanitation, drainage, water supply, waste management, public spaces, structural improvements and energy efficiency can improve housing conditions while allowing communities to retain their livelihoods, social networks and cultural identity. This principle is especially important in historic neighborhoods.
Bangladesh ultimately needs to move from counting houses to measuring housing adequacy. A national framework could assess affordability, tenure security, habitability, basic services, accessibility, location, climate resilience, and social and cultural adequacy. These dimensions could also be mapped through GIS to identify neighborhoods where different forms of housing deprivation overlap and where place-specific interventions are needed.
This would shift the housing conversation from “How many units have we built?” to a much more meaningful question: “Are people actually able to live well in those homes?”
World Habitat Day should therefore prompt us to ask a different question. Not simply: How many houses does Bangladesh need? We should ask: Can a family afford its home without sacrificing food, education or healthcare? Can a worker reach employment without losing hours every day? Can a child study safely at home? Can a tenant live without constant insecurity? Can an elderly person reach essential services? Can a community survive both climate risks and redevelopment pressures?
If the answer is no, providing a roof is not enough. For Bangladesh, “Adequate Housing for All” should not remain an annual slogan. It should become a principle that guides how we plan our cities, invest in infrastructure, regulate rental markets, respond to climate risks and measure development itself. Because the real success of housing policy will not ultimately be counted in apartments, plots or buildings. It will be measured by whether those homes allow people to live with security, dignity and opportunity.
Mowtushi Poit is Assistant Professor, Bangladesh Institute of Governance and Management (BIGM).

item.title: Our road safety and the ticket of poverty to endanger others without consequence. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Picture your own evening in Dhaka. You leave work tired and reach a busy crossing. Your child waits beside you, holding your hand. A battery powered rickshaw comes straight at you on the wrong side of the road.
It has no number plate. Its driver holds no licence. No fitness test has ever checked its brakes. You pull your child back, and it rushes past. You breathe out and cross, because there is no other way home.
The Bangladesh Road Transport Authority estimates that 10 to 12 lakh of these vehicles run in this city, though no office holds an exact count. Some evenings, someone does not pull back in time. The driver who hits them will most likely never face a conviction.
The scale is not a matter of opinion. Road accidents killed 9,111 people and injured 14,812 others across Bangladesh in 2025, a nearly six percent rise over the previous year. In Dhaka alone, 1,384 people were killed in road crashes between 2020 and July this year , and pedestrians, the people with no vehicle and no fault, made up 42.77 percent of the dead. Auto-rickshaws, CNG three-wheelers, and legunas together were involved in well over a tenth of all recorded crashes in that same stretch. These are abstractions. More so, they are people crossing a road that never had a working signal.
Ask anyone who commutes through Kuril, Mirpur, or Gulistan on a given evening, and battery rickshaws will come up before anything else does.
The Bangladesh Power Development Board estimates that 45 to 50 lakh battery powered rickshaws and easy bikes now operate nationwide , most outside any formal registry. Dhaka's new AI powered traffic camera system , launched this year to automatically fine violators, has run into exactly this wall.
Cameras can identify a bus or a car by its plate, but most auto-rickshaws carry no digital plate at all, so the system cannot see them. Drivers know it. Wrong way movement on routes such as 300 Feet Road, Kuril-Badda, and Moghbazar continues largely unpunished, because the tool built to catch it cannot legally identify the offender.
This is not a story of reckless individuals alone. It is a story of a vehicle class that grew faster than any ministry chose to regulate it, because regulating it would mean confronting the livelihoods of millions of low income drivers at once.
Even editorial voices now conceding the need for authorized manufacturing, registration, and defined routes warn against a blanket crackdown that would strip a poor driver of his only income overnight. Both things are true simultaneously.
That is precisely the trap.
Move from three-wheelers to buses and trucks and the same pattern holds.
A 2025 investigation found that 63.29 percent of people seeking BRTA services had to pay a bribe , and unskilled drivers routinely buy what insiders call a contract licence, a stamp of competence with no test behind it.
A driver earning a few thousand taka a month cannot afford the weeks a proper licensing process demands, so he pays the shortcut instead, and the owner who hires him never asks for a genuine result, because a cheap, undertrained driver saves the owner money either way.
Here poverty stops being an excuse and becomes a shield. Only about five percent of road accident cases in Bangladesh end in conviction . The maximum sentence for causing death through reckless driving once stood at seven years .
In 1985, after truckers protested, the Ershad government cut it to three, where it remains. Compensation follows the same script. The Road Transport Act 2018 quietly replaced a victim's right to sue an owner in court with a right to merely apply for aid from a state fund, and today only around five percent of victims ever receive a payout , capped at five lakh taka for a death regardless of fault.
Lawmakers assumed, correctly in most cases, that a driver or owner cannot afford a real settlement, so the state built a shared fund instead of individual liability, quietly telling every reckless driver that poverty, his own and his employer's, will absorb the cost of whoever he kills.
This pattern is not unique to us. Research on paratransit across the developing world finds the same feature everywhere, informal three-wheelers filling gaps formal transit leaves behind, operating with almost no oversight, and the resulting safety costs landing hardest on the poorest road users. What varies is how seriously a government decides to close that gap.
The people dying under these wheels are, overwhelmingly, just as poor as the men driving them.
This is poverty killing poverty, while transport owners' associations that resist digitized licensing and oppose stricter fitness checks sit comfortably above it all.
Real reform is not sympathy for reckless driving. It is mandatory digital plates and a real national registry for every battery rickshaw on the road, so an AI camera can finally see what it is built to catch.
It is an enforceable right to sue, so liability lands on the owner, not the driver he underpays. It is a compensation fund that pays out in weeks, not years, and scales with fault.
Until then, poverty will keep functioning exactly as it does now on our roads, not as a tragedy the state is fighting, but as a ticket the state has already priced in.
AKM Lutfur Rahman is a Commonwealth Scholar, Road Safety Expert, and experienced Transport Director having held high-impact positions at the British High Commission, CARE Bangladesh, and in roles affiliated with the US Embassy. Nafis Ehsas Chowdhury is Officer, Corporate HR & OD at Ha-Meem Group and an Independent Columnist.

item.title: Israel's deepening diplomatic isolation after 3 years of genocide in Gaza. [ dawn ]
item.description:
After three years of Israel’s genocide in Gaza that has killed tens of thousands, Tel Aviv’s relations with its traditional Asian allies have increasingly fractured, deepening its diplomatic isolation.

A recent illustration of that isolation came at the UN General Assembly late last month, where Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cut a lonely figure as scores of delegates walked out of his speech.

The departing delegates included representatives from Asian nations such as Pakistan, Malaysia, Indonesia and Bangladesh.

Here is a look at how Asian countries have responded to Israel and the Gaza war.

East Asia

Israel has faced strong state-level criticism from its longtime East Asian allies, such as Japan and South Korea.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi opposed US sanctions against International Criminal Court (ICC) President Tomoko Akane, who sought an arrest warrant for Netanyahu over alleged war crimes in Gaza.

Takaichi reaffirmed Tokyo’s consistent support for the ICC during the UN General Assembly, pushing back against pressure from the US, and saying that the country takes the US sanctions against Akane “very seriously.”

Washington sanctioned Akane, the first Japanese national to head the ICC, in August, accusing the court of encroaching on state sovereignty.

With Seoul, tensions began in April after South Korean President Lee Jae Myung shared a video on social media alleging that Israeli soldiers abused a Palestinian child and then threw him off a rooftop.

Lee said it was necessary to determine the authenticity of the video and assess what actions were taken, stressing the seriousness of the allegations.

“Wartime homicide is no different from matters that we take issue with, such as the forced [enslavement of] comfort women, and the massacre of Jewish people,” he said.

The issue of “comfort women” refers to the sexual enslavement of thousands of women and girls, many of them Korean, by the Imperial Japanese Army during World War II.

Israel strongly criticised Lee for posting the video, calling it “unacceptable.”

Israel’s Foreign Ministry claimed that Lee relied on a “fake account” and had revived an incident from 2024 that had already been investigated. The ministry also accused Lee of trivialising the massacre of Jews on the eve of Holocaust Remembrance Day in Israel.

China, which has long supported a two-state solution, continued to reiterate its call.

President Xi Jinping said the two-state solution is the “right direction” for resolving the longstanding Palestine issue.

South and Southeast Asia

Sri Lanka, one of the first countries to recognise the State of Palestine, called at the UN General Assembly for the “early” recovery and reconstruction of Gaza, reiterating its support for Palestinians’ “inalienable” rights and a two-state solution.

“Recovery and reconstruction of Gaza must be an early priority,” Sri Lankan Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath said in his address, adding that Colombo supports resolving the Palestine issue in line with the 1967 borders.

Pakistan, a member of the Gaza Board of Peace, also reiterated its “unwavering” support for the Palestinian people and the establishment of an independent State of Palestine based on the pre-1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital.

Addressing the UN General Assembly, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said that Palestine must also be granted full membership in the UN.

India, for its part, continued to pursue its strategy of maintaining diplomatic and strategic ties with Israel while continuing to express traditional support for a two-state solution and Palestinian statehood.

India under Prime Minister Narendra Modi has significantly deepened its strategic relationship with Israel, including through Modi’s February meeting with Netanyahu, when the two countries elevated their ties to a “Special Strategic Partnership”.

According to Jatin Desai, a Mumbai-based political analyst, India has historically stood with the Palestinian people. He said India’s position was clear even before the establishment of Israel.​​​​​​​

Thailand, which has maintained long-standing ties with Israel, continues to cooperate closely with Israel, particularly in agriculture and education.

Every year, around 100,000 Israeli tourists travel to Thailand, and thousands of Thai workers, both skilled and unskilled, are employed in Israel. The country is also a popular destination for Thai students pursuing academic studies.

Bangkok established diplomatic relations with Israel in 1954, while it officially recognised Palestine in 2012.

Pacific nations

In January, US President Donald Trump, as chair of the Board of Peace, invited Australia, Vietnam and Thailand to join the international body.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Canberra would consider the offer, though no decision had so far been taken.

“We’ve received correspondence from the president that arrived, I think, last night. That’s something we haven’t had time to consider. We’ll consider all of these approaches respectfully and through our proper processes,” Albanese said after receiving the invitation.

Thailand said it was reviewing the details of the offer, while Vietnam’s Communist Party General Secretary To Lam accepted Trump’s invitation to join the Gaza Peace Council and “affirmed Vietnam’s readiness to participate as a founding member state of the council”.

New Zealand, which did not join neighbouring Australia and other European nations in recognising the State of Palestine last year, said recognition of Palestinian statehood is “inevitable”.

In his final speech as Wellington’s foreign minister in the incumbent government earlier this month, Winston Peters said his decision in 2025 not to join most other UN member states in recognising Palestine was an example of truly independent foreign policy.

The Pacific, a cluster of small island nations, has provided Israel with a bloc of supportive voices in international forums, even as global criticism intensifies and more countries move to recognise Palestine.

Fiji further strengthened ties with Israel in September 2025 by opening a new embassy in Jerusalem. Days earlier, it abstained in a UN vote on a two-state solution. Like many of its neighbours, Fiji does not recognise Palestine.

Papua New Guinea followed a similar path. In September 2023, it also opened an embassy in Jerusalem and has since repeatedly opposed calls for a ceasefire at the UN. The country continues to reject recognition of Palestinian statehood.

Nauru has long been a loyal supporter of Israel. It recognised Jerusalem as Israel’s capital in 2019 and, in September last year, voted against a resolution backing a two-state solution.

Palau and Micronesia have consistently voted in line with Israel at the UN.

Samoa signed a visa-waiver deal in 2019 but took a slightly different line in September last year, when it abstained in the two-state resolution. Still, like most of its neighbours, it has not recognised Palestine.

Other Pacific nations such as Vanuatu, the Marshall Islands, Kiribati, the Solomon Islands, Tuvalu and Tonga maintain diplomatic relations with Israel, regularly support it at UN forums and do not recognise Palestine.

Tonga and Israel signed a visa-waiver agreement in 2010, while Vanuatu and the Marshall Islands have consistently backed Israel in UN votes.

item.title: Bangladesh Pacer Hasan says Test cricket momentum turning for the Tigers. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Fast-rising pace bowler Hasan Mahmud said on Monday Bangladesh’s upward trajectory has made a place in the World Test Championship final a realistic dream for his team.

Bangladesh are fourth in the World Test Championship standings after a shock nine-wicket victory over Australia in Darwin in August, a result that highlighted the strides made by a side long regarded as Test underachievers.

“The momentum is coming towards us, definitely,” Hasan, 26, told AFP in an interview in Dhaka.

“The atmosphere is such that Bangladesh can now dominate in Test cricket,” said the right-arm bowler, who played a key role by taking 6-55 in Darwin.

“We haven’t dominated (in Test cricket). Now is the time.”

Hasan said the Darwin victory could be a springboard for bigger achievements for Bangladesh, who have won six of their 13 Tests in the past two years.

Bangladesh have six Tests remaining in the current World Test Championship cycle, including home series against the West Indies and England, as well as a tour of South Africa.

“If we win four matches at home, why shouldn’t we play in the World Test Championship final? That’s the dream for Bangladesh now,” Hasan said.

The paceman, who enjoyed a successful county stint with Kent this year, has been a central figure in Bangladesh’s recent rise.

Nicknamed “Mini-McGrath” after the Australian great Glenn McGrath, he believes the perception of Bangladeshi pace bowling is changing as the South Asian country produces a new generation of quicks.

“Since we started playing, the thinking has changed,” he said.

“They now realise Bangladesh also has good-quality fast bowlers who can be world-class.” Hasan’s aggressive approach was evident during the Australia series, where he focused on building pressure on batsmen.

“I was just doing my job and bowling. I wasn’t giving them anything easy to hit. I would attack them with the short ball and keep bowling my way. If they hit me, they hit me,” he said.

Bangladesh were unable to clinch the two-Test series, with Australia claiming the second Test in Mackay by an innings and 51 runs.

However, Hasan said he was confident that Bangladesh’s “graph will continue to move upward” in the coming days.

“Look at how much we’ve improved in Test cricket,” he said.

“If the fast bowlers stay in good shape and the batsmen remain in form, then we will go to a higher level. “

item.title: A question for teachers. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
“A man without an aim is like a ship without a radar.” Almost each and every one of us has written this line at some point in our academic life, usually in a paragraph or an essay titled “Aim in life.”
There is nothing wrong with the sentence. A person should certainly have a direction in life. But the real problem came afterwards.
Why did our ships become the same? Why did they all sail towards the same destination? Can everyone’s aim in life really be the same? Perhaps this is where the failure began, passing from one generation to another.
From class 6 or so, we started writing about our aim in life. In Bangladesh, we traditionally followed specific grammar and composition books, guidebooks, and teachers’ notes. Teachers often provided model answers and encouraged students to follow them because those answers were considered safe for examinations and could help students get good marks.
What were we actually writing?
If I am not wrong, there were usually three popular aims in life: Doctor, engineer, and teacher. We did not have to think too much. The professions were already available. We only had to choose one and memorize the paragraph.
The doctor would return to his native village and provide free medical treatment to poor people.
The engineer would contribute to the development of the country.
The teacher would educate the nation and build the future generation.
The stories were almost identical. Only the handwriting was different.
Having some experience in school teaching, I have seen the most ironic part of it. A student from a commerce background is still writing: “I want to become a doctor.”
Does the student genuinely want to become a doctor? Probably not. Because that is what the student has been taught to write in the exam.
Why is this problematic?
The whole idea becomes problematic when we ask children to decide their future by memorizing a model answer.
Why should everyone become a doctor and then go back to their native village to provide free medical service? How would they earn a living? How would they build a career?
And if everyone became a doctor, engineer, or teacher, who would become the banker, entrepreneur, journalist, farmer, designer, or researcher?
We never discussed these questions. The purpose was to write something that would satisfy the examiner.
And then comes the bigger question: How many of us actually reached the destination we wrote about? How many of those students became doctors and engineers? What happened to the rest?
Perhaps the student who wrote, “I want to become a doctor,” eventually became a teacher. Another became an artist, a businessman, a journalist, or a photographer. Someone started a restaurant. Someone left the country. Someone became a parent and devoted his or her life to raising a family.
Did they fail? Of course not. They simply discovered their passion or a different destination.
And this is where I want to ask our teachers a question. What if a student today writes, “I want to become a YouTuber or an influencer”? What if they write “chef”, “singer”, “cricketer”, “footballer”, “content creator”, “gamer”, or “entrepreneur?”
Would you immediately consider these answers less respectable than “doctor” or “engineer?”
Perhaps some teachers would say that children need realistic ambitions. Some may argue that social media careers are uncertain and that students should focus on traditional professions.
There is certainly a valid concern here. Not every ambition will become a sustainable career, and students need guidance about the realities of different professions.
But guidance and imposition are not the same thing. A teacher’s responsibility should not be to tell every student where the ship must go. It should be to teach the student how to navigate, read the map, understand the risks, and choose a destination.
The world has changed dramatically since many of us were students. New professions have emerged. The way people work has changed.
A young person can now earn a living through skills that did not even exist as recognized professions some years earlier.
Yet our classrooms sometimes continue to operate with the same old list of acceptable dreams.
Perhaps it is time to change the answer. Perhaps it is also time to change the way we evaluate the answer.
A student does not necessarily have to write what we expect to see.
Maybe the problem is not that students have the wrong dreams. Maybe we have been evaluating their dreams with the wrong expectations.
Maybe we should be more interested in understanding why a student has chosen a particular goal.
It should be a student’s own answer to a very difficult question: “What do I want to do with my life?”
Md Inzamul Haque is a lecturer at the Department of English, Southeast University. He can be reached at inzamul.haque@seu.edu.bd .
