item.title: Helping teachers teach. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Today, we observe World Teachers’ Day under Unesco’s global call to value teacher voices and transform education. For Bangladesh, this day must be looked at as a moment of collective reflection when it comes to education, and how we support educators across all levels.
Any education system is only as strong as its educators. Yet for decades, our classrooms have suffered from chronic underfunding, politicization, and systemic administrative neglect.
If we are to build an equitable, knowledge-driven society, empowering and supporting our teachers must become the bedrock of national policy.
This starts with having an adequate budget for the sector as a whole, something we have struggled with as a nation.
When yearly budgets allocate insufficient funds for education, it signals to the rest of the country that it is a sector not worth investing in, despite the lofty claims of it being the backbone of a nation. The present government has rightfully been commended for increasing the allocation, but having more money is only the first step.
For teachers, the lack of continuous, high-quality pedagogical training and modern digital tools also remain barriers, and it is students who suffer as a result.
Furthermore, the persistent practice of politicizing teacher recruitment, promotions, and school governing bodies has eroded academic meritocracy, discouraging passionate talent from entering the profession.
Rote learning, outdated syllabi, and severe disparities in learning outcomes between urban and rural areas continue to leave millions of students unprepared for the demands of a globalized economy, and it is good teachers who will be able to begin fixing these deep-rooted issues.
Restoring the integrity of our education system requires treating teachers not as administrative instruments but as essential architects of our nation’s future.
As such, instituting comprehensive structural reforms and ensuring the continuous investment in our educators is among the most vital investments in our nation’s potential. Let this day serve as a firm commitment to give our teachers the dignity, resources, and respect they truly deserve.

item.title: Rethinking urban living. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
With October 5 being recognized as World Habitat Day, and under the United Nations theme "Adequate Housing for All," Bangladesh must face its inescapable urban crisis.
In a rapidly urbanizing nation where millions of people reside in informal settlements in our major cities, the right to adequate shelter remains a distant promise for a vast segment of our population.
Housing is not merely a roof overhead but encompasses basic sanitation, clean drinking water, and safety. For millions of low-income families, the absence of these basic conditions represents a daily struggle for human dignity.
Our urban planning apparatus has long suffered from a deep structural imbalance. While high-end residential real estate and luxury high-rises dominate development plans, affordable housing for the working poor receives little more than token budgetary allocations.
This disparity is compounded by sprawling slum settlements prone to frequent fires and severe vulnerability to seasonal natural disasters. Given the impact of climate change, flooding and erosion displace rural households daily and our major cities are forced to absorb thousands of new arrivals without the infrastructure to house them safely.
Addressing this deficit therefore will require moving past ad-hoc interventions. The state must treat housing as a fundamental social right and a public good.
Delivering "adequate housing for all" demands integrated and planned urban development -- including low-cost public housing projects, long-term rental assistance, slum-upgrading initiatives, and decentralized urban planning to ease pressure on the capital and other major cities.
Urban sustainability cannot be achieved while millions remain functionally unhoused or trapped in hazardous living environments. We need the authorities concerned to enact inclusive housing policies that prioritize marginalized populations.
Ensuring safe, dignified, and climate-resilient shelter for every citizen is not an impossible ideal but a prerequisite for a stable, equitable, and humane nation.

item.title: Rethinking public sector management and governance. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The existing career planning wing of the Ministry of Public Administration performs an important administrative role, but it should not be expected to substitute for a dedicated research-oriented mechanism with a broader mandate for evidence-based human-resource policy.
The HRRC could also study patterns of posting, transfer, promotion, disciplinary action, training opportunities, and leadership selection to identify systemic weaknesses and develop objective policy recommendations.
Such a mechanism could help ensure that individual professional experiences are transformed into institutional learning rather than remaining isolated personal stories.
From administrative control to results-based governance
Public-sector management should ultimately be measured by outcomes.
Citizens do not experience government through organizational charts or administrative procedures. They experience government through the services they receive, the fairness of public institutions, the accessibility of government programmes, and the responsiveness of officials.
Therefore, public-sector reform should increasingly emphasise:
Inputs → Processes → Outputs → Outcomes → Public Value
This requires stronger performance management, better coordination, effective use of data, digital transformation, institutional accountability, and continuous evaluation.
The objective should be to move from a culture of procedural compliance alone towards a culture of results, responsiveness, and public value.
My experience in managing development projects also demonstrated that safeguarding public resources is an essential component of results-based governance.
While serving as additional secretary, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, I also served, in addition to my regular responsibilities, as project director of the CECCR project, now associated with the development of the National Institute of Environment and Climate Change (NIECC).
During my tenure, an endowment fund accumulated under the project attracted attention from senior quarters. I took the position that the funds could not be utilized except in accordance with applicable rules and for their intended institutional purpose.
Subsequently, I was withdrawn from the project before its completion and another officer was assigned responsibility. From my professional perspective, this was an unusual development because project directors would ordinarily continue until project completion, the end of their tenure, or a legitimate public-interest requirement for reassignment.
Nevertheless, I continued to regard the protection of the public interest as the overriding consideration.
An important outcome of that period was the mobilization of approximately Tk10 crore from the Bangladesh Climate Change Trust (BCCT) in accordance with the applicable procedures and the preservation of the funds through fixed deposits with Agrani Bank at the relevant time.
The subsequent institutional evolution of CECCR (currently NIECC), provides an important example of why public resources must be protected even when such decisions may be inconvenient to powerful interests.
Results-based governance is not simply about completing projects. It is also about ensuring that public resources remain protected, traceable, and available for their intended institutional purpose.
Citizen-centred governance
Good governance ultimately depends upon the relationship between the state and its citizens.
Citizens need institutions that are accessible, predictable, transparent, fair, and responsive.
Citizen-centred governance therefore requires public agencies to understand citizens’ needs and evaluate service delivery from the perspective of users rather than solely from the perspective of administrative procedures.
This includes reducing unnecessary administrative burdens, strengthening grievance-redress mechanisms, improving digital services, ensuring equitable access, and making public institutions more responsive to vulnerable and marginalised communities.
Effective field administration requires not merely issuing administrative orders but understanding local realities, responding to grievances, coordinating government agencies, and ensuring that public programs reach intended beneficiaries.
Such reforms can strengthen citizens’ trust in government and reinforce the legitimacy of public institutions.
Public financial management and institutional accountability
Strong public-sector management also requires responsible management of public resources.
Public financial management should be closely connected with governance objectives through:
During my tenure as MD of Jiban Bima Corporation, I sought to strengthen governance in the areas of financial management, administration, business development, and streamlined service delivery.
At one stage, however, serious concerns arose regarding an actuarial valuation undertaken in connection with the Bangladesh Insurance Sector Development Project (BISDP). An external firm was engaged in the process, and the valuation reportedly generated a liability figure of approximately Tk11,00 crore for Jiban Bima Corporation.
In accordance with the applicable provisions of the Insurance Act, 2010, the JBC liabilities, determined through another agency’s valuation, were not accepted during my tenure. Consequently, I incurred the personal wrath of the FID Secretary and Chairman IDRA. These individuals and certain quarters were to establish an exorbitant liability against the Jiban Bima Corporation through an unlawfully executed actuarial valuation, thereby gradually destroying the state-owned corporation and causing private insurance to flourish.
I therefore considered it essential that any such process involving a state-owned insurance corporation should be conducted strictly in accordance with the applicable legal and regulatory framework, with appropriate institutional authorization and accountability.
There is a broader institutional question here: Can a public-sector manager be expected to protect public resources and uphold regulatory standards if doing so exposes the officer to professional retaliation?
This question deserves serious consideration in any discussion of public-sector governance reform.
The lesson is not that individual officers should confront institutional authority. The lesson is that public institutions should create systems in which legitimate disagreement, professional advice, audit concerns, and regulatory objections can be raised without fear of arbitrary retaliation.
Institutional accountability and the protection of public resources
The experience of public-sector management also demonstrates that accountability must extend beyond the individual officer responsible for a decision.
For example, where government vehicles, fuel, project resources, or other public assets are used outside approved rules, the resulting financial burden ultimately falls upon the public.
During my involvement with project management, I observed concerns regarding the use of project vehicles and associated fuel expenditure. Such matters should be addressed through transparent administrative controls, audit mechanisms, and the oversight of the appropriate steering or governing committees.
The responsibility for ensuring such accountability should not rest solely with an individual project director. The relevant ministry, steering committee, audit authorities, and senior administrative leadership all have roles to play.
Institutional accountability therefore must be systemic rather than selective.
Where rules exist but are inconsistently enforced, institutional credibility is weakened. Where audit objections can be neutralised through informal influence, public financial management becomes vulnerable.
Effective governance therefore requires not only rules, but also credible mechanisms for enforcing those rules.
A reform agenda
A comprehensive public-sector management reform agenda could focus on the following priorities:
1. Strengthen the rule of law and regulatory enforcement
Ensure that laws are applied consistently, fairly, and predictably.
2. Institutionalize merit-based human-resource management
Strengthen objective criteria for recruitment, promotion, posting, and professional development.
3. Strengthen civil service training
Move from predominantly procedural training towards competency-based, continuous professional development.
4. Establish the HRRC
Create an evidence-based institutional mechanism for strategic civil-service human-resource research.
5. Strengthen performance management
Link professional development and institutional accountability to measurable performance and results.
6. Promote ethical and professional leadership
Develop leadership standards that emphasize integrity, competence, accountability, and public service.
7. Protect administrative professionalism
Maintain an appropriate balance between political accountability and professional civil-service neutrality.
8. Establish safeguards against arbitrary personnel actions
Ensure that transfers, postings, promotions, and disciplinary measures are based on transparent institutional criteria rather than informal influence.
9. Strengthen citizen-centred service delivery
Measure public institutions by the quality and accessibility of services delivered to citizens.
10. Promote evidence-based policy-making
Increase the use of administrative data, research, evaluation, and comparative international experience.
11. Strengthen public financial management
Ensure that public resources are protected through effective procurement, internal controls, audit, and transparent financial reporting.
12. Strengthen institutional continuity
Ensure that public-sector institutions remain effective across political and administrative transitions.
Way forward
Bangladesh’s future development will depend not only on economic resources or infrastructure but also on the strength and quality of its public institutions.
The central challenge is therefore to build a public sector that is capable, ethical, meritocratic, accountable, innovative, and citizen-centred.
My own experience over a long career in public administration has convinced me that institutional integrity is tested most severely when lawful professional judgment comes into conflict with powerful interests.
I encountered circumstances in which adherence to rules and public interest was not always consistent with the preferences of influential individuals.
On several occasions, refusing to accommodate what I considered improper requests resulted in pressure, threats, investigations, or transfers.
Yet these experiences reinforced, rather than weakened, my conviction that public officials must remain guided by law, evidence, professional ethics, and the public interest.
Citizens are more likely to respect laws when laws are consistently enforced. Public servants are more likely to perform professionally when institutions reward competence and integrity. Governments are more likely to achieve sustainable development when public institutions possess the capacity to translate policy commitments into measurable outcomes.
A strong state does not depend on powerful individuals. It depends on strong institutions.
Bangladesh therefore needs a public administration capable of combining democratic accountability with professional competence, political responsiveness with administrative integrity, and procedural discipline with results-oriented management.
At the same time, civil servants who act according to law and protect public resources should receive institutional protection. Professional integrity cannot be sustained if officers are expected to act ethically but remain vulnerable to arbitrary retaliation for doing so.
Strengthening public-sector human resources should therefore be at the centre of this transformation. The proposed Human Resources Research Cell could contribute to this agenda by providing the evidence, analysis, and institutional perspective necessary for long-term civil-service reform.
Ultimately, public administration is not simply about managing government offices. It is about managing the institutional capacity through which the state serves its people.
Our ancestors rest in this soil, and one day we too will return to it. The enduring measure of public service should therefore be what institutions we strengthen, what public value we create, what public resources we protect, and what standards of integrity we leave behind.
Building capable, accountable, and trusted public institutions is not merely an administrative objective. It is a foundation for sustainable national development and a lasting obligation to future generations.
Md Mizanul Hoque Chowdhury is Former Additional Secretary, Ministry of Public Administration, Bangladesh.

item.title: Is grass really green on the other side?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
In tea stalls across Dhaka, scrollable feeds on smartphones, and family dinner tables nationwide, a singular refrain echoes with predictable cadence: "Leaving the country is the only way out."
Faced with persistent domestic headwinds -- sticky inflation squeezing household budgets, job market stagnation, and concerns over personal security -- the instinct to seek greener pastures abroad has morphed from an ambition into a standard reflex.
Yet, as thousands of young professionals, students, and workers pack their hopes into polished suitcases, they confront a quiet, uncomfortable truth: The global exit door is closing fast.
For a nation of over 170 million people, leaving is no longer a simple matter of ambition; it has become an intricate, exhausting bottleneck.
The harsh reality is that leaving Bangladesh has become almost as difficult as staying -- raising a fundamental question about how we view our collective future.
The ordeal begins long before anyone reaches an international departure terminal. In Bangladesh, the journey abroad starts in government offices, defined by bureaucratic red tape.
Obtaining basic personal credentials -- a birth certificate, a national ID correction, utility-backed address proofs, and eventually a passport -- often becomes a trial of endurance.
Simple typographical errors on a primary school certificate can initiate months of administrative hurdles.
Citizens navigate multiple desks, enduring lengthy delays and arbitrary verification steps just to secure the legal right to apply for a visa.
Before an applicant ever faces a foreign consular officer, their energy and financial resources are significantly drained by domestic administrative processes.
The credibility gap and visa rejections
Even when documentation is complete, foreign embassies present steep hurdles.
Bangladeshi passport holders face exceptionally high visa rejection rates, even for routine travel or higher education.
This trust deficit has not emerged in a vacuum.
Decades of irregular migration, widespread forgery of bank statements and educational certificates by predatory middlemen, and a tendency for individuals to overstay visitor or student visas to seek asylum have damaged the country's international standing.
International immigration authorities now scrutinize applications from Bangladesh with heightened skepticism.
As a result, ordinary students and legitimate professionals pay the price for systemic abuses.
Work visas across traditional labour destinations in the Middle East and Southeast Asia face periodic freezes, while Western nations tighten student intake quotas and financial proof requirements.
The green passport -- frequently ranked near the bottom of global mobility indexes -- reflects a serious credibility issue that limits legitimate opportunities.
Competitiveness gap
Beyond administrative barriers lies a deeper structural issue: Market readiness.
Modern global labour markets demand high specialization, research literacy, fluent communication, and rapid technical adaptation.
In these areas, Bangladesh struggles with persistent gaps.
While neighbouring nations in South Asia have systematically aligned their primary, vocational, and tertiary education systems with global standards, Bangladesh’s educational framework remains fragmented.
Despite years of compulsory English education, many graduates struggle with professional fluency, creating immediate communication barriers during embassy interviews, university applications, and workplace interactions.
Furthermore, tertiary institutions in Bangladesh rarely rank at all in global university lists, leaving graduates at a disadvantage when competing against international peers.
In an era where artificial intelligence and automation are reshaping global workplaces, Bangladeshi jobseekers often lag in leveraging digital tools and AI-driven productivity workflows.
While global candidates use advanced tech stacks to secure remote work or specialized roles, many Bangladeshi applicants remain reliant on traditional skill sets that are rapidly becoming obsolete.
The friction extends beyond skills to international perceptions.
Due to publicized cases of document fraud and irregular migration routes, foreign governments have implemented stricter border policies.
Consulates that once processed thousands of students and work permits annually have raised financial thresholds, reduced quotas, or relocated their processing centers altogether, requiring applicants to travel to neighbouring countries just for an interview.
This institutional skepticism makes the migration process prohibitively expensive and uncertain, turning what used to be a viable career pathway into an unpredictable gamble.
This reality creates a challenging dilemma for young Bangladeshis.
At home, economic pressures are real: High inflation erodes purchasing power, job creation struggles to keep pace with university output, and social security challenges persist.
Yet the alternative abroad is rarely the seamless transition depicted on social media.
Immigrants frequently encounter skyrocketing costs of living, tight housing markets, strict work-hour caps for students, and the constant strain of maintaining legal status.
The realization that life abroad carries its own severe challenges can be discouraging for those who view migration as a guaranteed solution.
Redefining the horizon
While these obstacles may seem daunting, recognizing them offers an important opportunity for recalibration.
The realization that leaving is not a universal solution forces a shift in focus back to building strength from within.
Bangladesh’s greatest asset remains its demographic dividend -- a young, resilient, and adaptive population.
If the path outward is restricted, the imperative shifts to building capacity domestically. This recalibration is already taking shape across several sectors:
The current mobility challenge does not signal the end of progress for Bangladesh's youth.
Rather, it marks the end of a reliance on simple exit strategies.
By shifting focus from escaping domestic challenges to developing competitive skills and improving local systems, the nation can build a context where staying is no longer seen as a compromise, but as a meaningful, viable choice.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Leave small businesses alone. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
There's a good argument that every business in the country should be registered -- so that we know who is doing what, who is obeying tax laws, and so on.
There's also a good argument for keeping really small businesses completely out of the bureaucratic system -- for really small businesses simply do not have the time, or often even the knowledge, to be able to deal with the bureaucracy.
As is obvious, these two arguments are in conflict with each other.
The correct error -- or at least I would insist, which is not quite the same thing as insisting I am correct to do so -- is to be on the side of allowing small businesses to escape the bureaucracy.
This is the background to the requirement that every business must now have a BIN -- a Business Identification Number.
The claim is that this requirement hits cottage, micro, small, and medium enterprises (CMSMEs) hard. It isn't that applying for the number is difficult. It's that it can be difficult to get the supporting documentation required to be able to make that application.
For example, a legal rental agreement -- or property deed - is required for the business address. Yet plenty of micro businesses run from the left hand side of the family dining table.
If we're talking about manufacturing, then it requires a machinery list, an equipment layout plan, and input-output coefficient information. There are people out there running perfectly fine businesses who don't know what that last part means, and I'm not sure I do either.
It's obvious what is happening here. The bureaucracy thinks it would be a fine thing if everyone in business were doing business correctly and in a formal and registered manner.
Thus they can use the need for a BIN to make sure that everyone is indeed doing things correctly -- working at a property licensed to run a business from, for example. For larger businesses, this could even be true too.
For smaller businesses -- micro, cottage, and so on -- these requirements can be the difference between it being worth being a legal business at all or remaining in the shadows of the grey economy.
Grey here meaning not illegal as a business -- that's the black economy. Just one that's not registered and paying taxes and such.
And here's the thing. We all want to have economic growth. That's how to climb that ladder from a less developed economy all the way up to a developed and rich one.
Economic growth comes from new business formation. Very little of total economic growth comes from large companies growing yet more.
Nearly all of it comes from someone using that corner of the kitchen table to come up with a new idea and trying it out.
Barriers to those tryouts limit, slow, or even stop, economic growth.
The correct answer, therefore, is to reverse that process of applying for the legality of the business.
Get people signed up for the BIN first. Say, if you have some form of personal ID, then you can apply online for that BIN.
Great, you're now a business and you can use that number to gain access to a bank account and all the rest.
We can worry about obeying all of the other laws -- when you need to provide a machinery layout plan, for example -- to when you're a large enough business that it's worth worrying about.
Yes, some people will abuse this reversal of the current process. But that's just the same argument as we started with.
It would be good if everyone was running every business according to all the rules. But the rules also prevent some people from starting up in business at all.
The error should be, again to my mind, on getting the business happening first -- for that's the part that makes us richer -- and worrying about compliance with all the bureaucratic laws later.
Adam Smith pointed out that the only things required to move from barbarism to the highest degree of opulence is peace, easy taxes, and the tolerable administration of justice.
That “tolerable” there means yes, of course everyone absolutely must obey the really important laws but a certain benign neglect of the details is also necessary.
Or even, as we can and should put it, less bureaucracy means more business. Let's err on the side of more business as that's the one that makes us richer.
Tim Worstall is a senior fellow at Adam Smith.

item.title: Your phone number is now your identity. Guard it. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
A shopkeeper in Mirpur comes home from Friday prayers and sees that his phone has no signal. He blames the network, as most of us would. By the time he gets to a service centre the next morning, his mobile wallet is empty, he's locked out of Facebook, and three of his cousins have received messages from "him" asking for money.
The shopkeeper is invented, but the sequence is a familiar one. And none of it took clever hacking. Whoever did this only needed his number.
It's worth stopping to think about how much a Bangladeshi phone number carries these days. It receives the one-time password for your wallet. It's how you get back into Facebook when you forget your password, how WhatsApp knows it's you, how the courier confirms your parcel.
Banks lean on it more every year. We built one of the most phone-dependent economies anywhere, and somewhere along the way, 11 digits became the key to nearly everything. Nobody planned it. It just happened.
Attackers noticed long before users did. In my years running security work in Silicon Valley, I saw them go after whatever opened the most doors, again and again. Here, that's the SIM.
Most of the time they don't even have to take it, because we hand it over.
Someone calls, says he's from your wallet provider, warns that your account will be suspended, and asks you to read out the code you've just received.
Or a message arrives: Sorry, I sent my code to your number by mistake, could you forward it?
These tricks work because Bangladeshis are, on the whole, helpful people who trust a polite voice.
A real provider will never ask for your PIN or OTP. Not by phone, not by SMS, and not through a relative who says the company told them to.
When a fraudster can't talk the code out of you, he may go after the SIM itself and get a replacement issued in your name.
Biometric SIM registration made that much harder. I worked on those systems, and it was a real step forward that many wealthier countries still haven't taken.
It didn't make it impossible, though. Forged papers, a bribed insider, or a careless recovery process can still get someone through.
What you'd notice is your phone going dead while everyone around you still has signal. Most people wait a day before dealing with that, and a day is more than enough.
Then there are the apps: A cracked game, an "update" someone forwarded on WhatsApp, a free copy of something that normally costs money.
Some of these ask to read your SMS, or to use Android's accessibility features, which were built for people with disabilities and let an app see and tap whatever is on your screen.
Say yes, and the app can read your OTPs as they arrive. You never share anything. It simply watches.
Start with the OTP. Treat it like cash, and don't give it to anyone, including someone who sounds exactly like a family member.
Put a PIN on WhatsApp through their two-step verification settings, which takes about two minutes.
If your signal drops for no obvious reason, call your operator from someone else's phone within the hour, and let your wallet provider know too.
Get your apps from the Play Store, and when a torch app asks to read your messages, ask yourself why.
Finally, have one conversation at home about a family code word, something only you would know, to ask for whenever money comes up. It sounds like something out of a movie, but it costs nothing and it works.
Still, it isn't fair to leave all of this to individuals. A phone number was never meant to prove who someone is on its own.
In several countries, banks and mobile operators have started passing each other one simple piece of information: Has this SIM been replaced in the past few days? If it has, the large transfer waits until someone checks.
Bangladesh has already done the hard part with biometric registration, so it could do this more easily than most.
The same thinking applies inside the phone. Security that catches a malicious app before it gets anywhere near a wallet or banking app should come as standard, rather than something people discover after they've been robbed.
October is Cybersecurity Awareness Month. We tend to measure how digital Bangladesh is by how many people are online. A better measure might be how many of them feel safe once they get there.
Everyone who loses money this way tells their family, their neighbours, the regulars at the tea stall. Each story makes the next person a little warier of going digital, and that wariness takes a long time to wear off.
The number is already our identity. We just haven't started treating it that way.
Zeeshan R Khan led a security practice at Cisco for more than 12 years and is based in Silicon Valley. He is the founder of SurroundApps, which builds mobile security and family-safety technology for Bangladesh.

item.title: Hasan Nawaz's fighting 96 against India in vain as Pakistan settle for Asian Games cricket silver. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Hasan Nawaz’s fighting 96 went in vain as Pakistan fell 19 runs short of India’s 212-run target to settle for silver in the Asian Games men’s cricket final at the Korogi Athletic Park in Nisshin, Japan on Saturday.

Hasan struck five fours and seven sixes in his 51-ball innings before being caught behind off Shivam Dube from the final ball of the match, with Pakistan finishing on 192 for six.

Needing 33 from the last over after reaching 179 for five, Pakistan kept their hopes alive when Hasan hit Dube for a boundary and then a six. But a yorker from the India all-rounder followed by two dot balls left Hasan needing four for his century from the final delivery.

He attempted to clear the infield but was caught by wicket-keeper Sanju Samson, ending an innings that had briefly brought Pakistan back into contention.

Hasan’s dismissal completed a remarkable recovery after Pakistan had been 39 for three after six overs. He and Saim Ayub put on 87 for the fourth wicket before Saim was dismissed for 29 off 22 balls in the 15th over.

Hasan had reached his half-century from 28 balls and continued to attack India’s spinners, particularly Ravi Bishnoi, who conceded 44 from his three overs.

Pakistan were 126 for three after 14 overs, requiring 86 from the last 36 balls, but Dube removed Saim and Abdul Samad in successive stages of the closing overs to keep India ahead.

Saim was caught by Washington Sundar at square leg for 29 after attempting to use Dube’s pace, while Samad made nine before being caught by Tilak Varma off Washington in the 18th over.

Despite those setbacks, Hasan continued the assault. He reached 68 from 36 balls after hitting Axar Patel for a six in the 16th over and then struck two fours in Dube’s next over, one of them coming through an edge after he flashed at a short, wide delivery.

Pakistan reached 160 for four after 17 overs, needing 52 from the final 18 balls.

Saad Masood kept the chase alive with two sixes in his unbeaten 12 off five balls, but Bumrah’s fourth over yielded only 11 runs, leaving Pakistan 33 short with six balls remaining.

Dube was given the final over and conceded a boundary and a six to Hasan, but his yorkers at the crucial moment denied Pakistan the chance to complete the chase.

India’s bowlers had earlier kept Pakistan under pressure after the batters had posted 211 for six.

Pakistan’s chase had begun brightly enough but lost momentum after Sahibzada Farhan and Usman Khan departed in successive overs.

Farhan made 10 off 11 balls before attempting a slog-sweep against Sundar and finding Patel at deep midwicket. Usman followed for three off six, slogging a fuller delivery from Patel to Dube at midwicket.

Maaz Sadaqat, who made 23 off 18 balls with three fours, was then caught by Sundar off Patel at the start of the seventh over to leave Pakistan 39 for three.

Hasan and Saim rebuilt the innings, taking Pakistan to 76 for three at the halfway stage. Hasan was then 26 off 18 and Ayub 12 off nine.

The pair accelerated through the middle overs, with Hasan reaching his half-century from 28 balls. Their 87-run partnership gave Pakistan a realistic chance of chasing India’s imposing total, but Dube’s dismissal of Saim at 126 proved a significant turning point.

Varma stars

India had earlier been propelled to 211 for six by Varma and Dube, who added 62 from 31 balls for the sixth wicket.

Varma remained unbeaten on 51 off 22 balls, striking three fours and four sixes, while Dube made 27 off 15 with two fours and two sixes.

India had lost three wickets between the eighth and 15th overs after making an explosive start, but the late partnership lifted them beyond 200.

Abhishek Sharma provided the initial impetus with 61 off 28 balls, hitting three fours and seven sixes. Vaibhav Sooryavanshi made 15 off nine before being caught by Usman off Saim, while Sanju Samson was dismissed for two by Ahmed Daniyal.

Shreyas Iyer made 21 off 24 balls and Ishan Kishan 20 off 18. Ishan fell to Arafat Minhas at 128, while Iyer was dismissed by Abrar Ahmed five runs later.

India reached 114 in the first 10 overs before adding 97 in the second half of the innings. Varma reached his half-century from 21 balls and remained unbeaten, while Dube was dismissed by Daniyal in the first ball of the final over.

For Pakistan, Arafat took two for 25 from three overs and Daniyal two for 43. Abrar took one for 29 and Saim one for 47. Saad and Sufyan Moqim went wicketless.

Sri Lanka took the bronze medal after beating Bangladesh by 63 runs in the third-place playoff.

item.title: Democracy cannot survive with a fearful press. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
That at least 162 journalists across the country faced attacks, threats, and legal harassment in 112 separate incidents over the past three months while performing their professional duties, according to a monitoring report by private research organization Media Initiative for Development (MID), should alarm us.
When members of the media are systematically targeted simply for documenting public events, investigating corruption, or asking uncomfortable questions, it signals a dangerous erosion of basic rights.
A nation striving to rebuild its democratic institutions cannot succeed while those tasked with holding power accountable operate under constant fear for their safety.
In any functioning democracy, an independent press serves as the eyes and ears of the public, tasked with providing citizens with the objective facts necessary to make informed decisions.
When media workers are assaulted by political cadres, intimidated by influential interest groups, or subjected to arbitrary legal harassment, it is not merely an attack on individual reporters but a direct assault on the public's right to know.
This hostility toward journalism reflects a deep-seated, systemic culture of intolerance that has unfortunately persisted across political transitions, and has only been exacerbated as a result of the technology-enabled society we live in today.
When law enforcement agencies fail to protect working journalists on the ground or, worse, turn a blind eye to political mobs targeting newsrooms, it creates a chilling effect that fosters self-censorship.
It goes without saying that a media environment gripped by fear cannot fulfill its democratic mandate. Protecting press freedom requires more than public declarations but rather demands physical security, legal safeguards, and an environment where journalists can report without fear of retribution.
Democracy cannot survive without truth, and truth cannot surface when the press is silenced.

item.title: Revenue generation needs long-term planning. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The International Monetary Fund’s critical assessment of the National Board of Revenue’s (NBR) latest reform roadmap exposes a fundamental truth that has been an issue for Bangladesh for years: Short term, superficial administrative adjustments cannot resolve our chronic fiscal woes.
Despite repeated pledges to modernize tax collection and broaden the revenue base, it is disappointing that the NBR remains crippled by structural loopholes, slow execution, and a reliance on ad-hoc targets.
For a country maintaining one of the lowest tax-to-GDP ratios in South Asia , hovering under 8%, we must stop treating tax reform as a bureaucratic compliance exercise rather than the national priority it is.
The IMF’s critique rightly targets the core flaws of our revenue architecture. Rather than pursuing systemic modernization through comprehensive digitization, structural decoupling of tax policy from enforcement, and the elimination of discretionary exemptions, the revenue authority routinely defaults to squeezing existing taxpayers.
Setting ambitious revenue targets without fixing systemic leakages or curbing widespread tax evasion yields predictable shortfalls year after year. Furthermore, the persistent delay in fully automating tax administration and streamlining VAT collection perpetuates an environment ripe for rent-seeking and corruption.
Bangladesh can no longer afford an inefficient revenue apparatus. With growing debt-servicing obligations, rising social spending needs, and critical infrastructure demands, sustainable fiscal health depends on a modern, equitable, and transparent tax system.
As such, we hope and expect those at NBR to recognize that we learn to plan for the long term. For that to happen, we must start focusing on high-income earners and corporate entities currently operating outside official channels, rather than overburdening compliant businesses and middle-class citizens through indirect taxation.
Real reform requires genuine political will, not administrative posturing to satisfy multilateral lenders. Until the government replaces half-hearted measures with deep, structural reform, our fiscal stability will remain shaky.

item.title: India-Pakistan blockbuster brings cricket fever to Japan baseball field. [ dawn ]
item.description:
One of sport’s fiercest rivalries descended on a sleepy corner of Japan on Saturday as India and Pakistan clashed in the men’s cricket final at the Asian Games on a converted baseball field.

The neighbours only meet in international tournaments because of long-running political tensions and matches between them typically attract television audiences of hundreds of millions back home.

The gold-medal encounter in a suburban park in Nagoya was a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for Indians and Pakistanis living in Japan.

They lined up hours before the game to get into the cosy 2,500-capacity purpose-built Korogi Athletic Park Stadium.

“I think this is never going to happen again, India against Pakistan in Japan,” long-time Nagoya resident Umer Dar, draped in a Pakistan flag, told AFP.

“I’m crazy about cricket but I never have the opportunity to watch it live because I’ve lived here for 26 years.”

The last time India and Pakistan collided was at the T20 World Cup in February, where they played in front of a sell-out 35,000 crowd in Sri Lanka.

The Asian Games setting was significantly more modest, with trees and a baseball pitcher’s mound just beyond the boundary.

The atmosphere was as passionate as ever though, with fans waving flags and cheering every ball from the temporary stands.

“We bought tickets three months back when they started selling them,” said Tokyo resident and India supporter Mohammed Kashim Raja.

“At the time it was easy but it became really difficult for others to get them.

“We heard that many people were selling them for high prices.”

Cricket is a niche sport in Japan and neutrals at the final appeared to be virtually non-existent.

‘Always crazy’

There was more of a casual crowd at the bronze-medal match between Sri Lanka and Bangladesh earlier, on a warm and sunny day.

Teachers Hiromi Niwa and Miki Kaede, both from nearby Gifu, said they knew nothing about cricket and had bought tickets out of curiosity.

After reading a free leaflet explaining the rules and watching some of the action, Kaede said it had been a “really fun” experience.

She was disappointed that their tickets did not get them into the final.

“We didn’t realise that India against Pakistan was such a big deal until we actually searched for it,” she said.

Cricket has a growing presence in Japan and the sport got a huge boost when India played their first-ever T20 international against Japan last week.

The historic match, celebrating 75 years of diplomatic relations, took place at Japan’s modest Sano International Cricket Ground outside Tokyo.

It was Japan’s first T20 game against a full-member nation, and they gave India a huge fright before losing by two runs in a rain-shortened match.

Kushal Gowda, an Indian fan living in Tokyo, said Japanese people were “trying to understand” cricket.

“We were trying to explain to our colleagues in our office and they were curious and keen to know what it was about,” he said.

“They kind of compared it with baseball.”

The crowd for the Asian Games final was overwhelmingly supporting India, with only a few Pakistan flags and shirts dotted around the ground.

A cheer went up when the gates opened to let fans in, and the party continued when the game began under clear skies.

“Even if it’s in Japan, the craze of India versus Pakistan is always there,” said Tokyo-based India fan Afroz Khan.

“Anywhere they play in the world, it’s always crazy.”

item.title: Universal registration key to sustainable health system and development. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Civil registration, specifically birth and death registration, serves as a primary legal identity of a citizen. Without these essential credentials, an individual remains practically invisible to the state, left to navigate a maze of systemic hurdles to access basic rights and public services.
In Bangladesh, however, nearly half the population exists outside this official framework. The national registration rates stand at a dismal 50% for births and 47% for deaths, lagging drastically behind regional and global averages.
This structural gap produces far-reaching consequences. A missing birth record means a child is absent from the central database, impairing national planning at its root. Without accurate demographic figures, health planners must operate blindfolded, unable to project precise vaccine quotas, identify areas with severe childhood malnutrition, or allocate pediatric specialists where they are most desperately needed.
Similarly, the absence of death registration dismantles the core health system of a nation. As public health experts emphasize, basic mortality data such as information about age, location, and causes of death functions as a nation's epidemiological compass. Lack of clear data on where non-communicable diseases like cardiovascular conditions, strokes, cancer, and diabetes strike hardest may misdirect millions of public funds into ineffective health infrastructure.
Real-time data forms an essential part of disease surveillance. Consider a scenario where several people in a remote village succumb to an unidentified fever. If these deaths are neither registered promptly nor assigned a cause, central authorities remain oblivious to an emerging viral outbreak. By the time news reaches the health ministry, a localized cluster may have already proliferated into an epidemic.
Furthermore, when crisis hits and life-saving vaccines or drugs must be distributed, unregistered, marginalized populations are systematically overlooked. Without a comprehensive database, any strategy to contain an epidemic is inherently flawed.
As a frontline victim of climate change, Bangladesh faces recurring cyclones, storm surges, and seasonal floods that routinely devastate its coastal margins. In the wake of a disaster, search-and-rescue teams face a critical question. How many are truly missing or dead? Without accurate local birth and death registries at the Union Parishad level, relief distribution and state rehabilitation funds quickly go astray.
Severe consequence occurs within the social safety net system. Failing to update death records in real time creates phantom beneficiaries on state rosters, while vulnerable women are often denied widow allowances because they lack an official death certificate for their deceased spouses. Consequently, the most impoverished and disaster-affected citizens are stripped of their basic state entitlements.
As a result, a question arises: Why does public participation in civil registration remain so sluggish? The answer lies in the structural loopholes of the Birth and Death Registration Act, 2004, compounded by bureaucratic complexities.
According to the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS), 67% of births now occur within healthcare facilities. Yet, existing law places no direct mandate on hospital authorities to execute registrations. Instead, parents are forced to undertake an arduous visit to Union Parishad or City Corporation offices, where they routinely encounter technical glitches on online portals, tedious error-correction procedures, and informal fee extortion. Discouraged, thousands walk away, leaving their children legally invisible.
Target 16.9 of the Sustainable Development Goals envisions universal legal identity for all by 2030. Time is running short, and Bangladesh remains significantly off track. Closing this gap requires urgent legal amendment. The Birth and Death Registration Act, 2004 must be revised to shift the legal obligation of recording births and deaths directly onto health facilities, ensuring every newborn is registered at birth.
Across the Asia-Pacific, nations that transferred this administrative duty from individuals to healthcare institutions have successfully achieved universal civil registration.
Parallel to legal reform, technological issues must be resolved. Civil registration must be promoted as a fundamental human right. Tackling field-level staffing shortages, upgrading registrar training, and enforcing institutional accountability are non-negotiable steps toward a functional system.
Civil registration is far more than a routine ledger or a string of digital digits. It is the structural backbone of resilient public health, sustainable development, and crisis management.
The choice before us is evident. Do we continue allowing millions of citizens to remain invisible, anchoring our future to an unreliable, data-starved system? Or do we leverage targeted legal reform and modern technology to build a secure, inclusive, and resilient Bangladesh by 2030? The time to act is now.
Mashiat Abedin is Coordinator, and ABM Zubair is Executive Director, PROGGA (Knowledge for Progress).

item.title: The new power that shapes the world. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Wars have traditionally been decided by soldiers, weapons, and economic strength. But the character of power is changing rapidly. In the modern world, information technology and communication have become strategic weapons as powerful as missiles, aircraft, or financial resources. The recent Iran conflict has demonstrated this reality with extraordinary clarity.
The most important question in a modern conflict is no longer simply who has more weapons. It is increasingly who knows more, who knows it faster, and who can communicate it more effectively.
Modern military operations have depended heavily on satellite imagery, electronic surveillance, artificial intelligence, drones, radar systems, cyber capabilities, and real-time communications. The United States has acknowledged striking Iranian radar, air-defense, maritime, and communications facilities -- illustrating how information and communication networks themselves have become critical strategic targets.
US officials have linked high-resolution satellite imagery obtained by Iran to improved targeting capabilities in attacks against American military facilities. Whatever the political controversy surrounding the allegation, the episode demonstrates one fundamental reality: Accurate information can dramatically increase the effectiveness of military power.
The lesson is even clearer in Ukraine. Satellite communication has become an essential part of battlefield operations. Starlink-based communications have been used to coordinate forces and drones, while Russia has attempted to disrupt the system through electronic warfare. Reuters reported in July 2026 that Russian forces were trying to jam Starlink to counter Ukrainian drone operations.
The battlefield is no longer confined to land, sea, and air. There is now a fourth battlefield -- the information and communication domain.
But technology alone cannot win every conflict. Information becomes meaningful only when human beings can interpret it correctly and communicate intelligently.
This brings us to the second great power of the modern age: Communication.
A crisis may begin with weapons, economic pressure, or political disagreement, but it can often be contained through communication. A telephone call between leaders, a diplomatic message, a trusted intermediary, or a carefully negotiated agreement can prevent a conflict from becoming a catastrophe.
The Iran crisis itself illustrates this paradox. Despite military confrontation, diplomatic channels have repeatedly remained important.
Even in September 2026, diplomacy remains central to managing the consequences of the conflict. Iran and the United Arab Emirates endorsed a BRICS statement calling for restraint, protection of civilians and safeguarding global trade and maritime stability.
Another contemporary example comes from Ukraine. Recent US-backed diplomatic efforts have brought Russian and Ukrainian representatives into renewed discussions concerning possible peace arrangements, energy infrastructure, grain shipments, and prisoner exchanges. No final settlement has emerged, but the process demonstrates that communication remains indispensable even when military confrontation continues.
The same principle applies outside warfare. In business, the company with the best product does not necessarily become the market leader. The winner is often the company that understands its customers fastest, uses data intelligently, and communicates its value most effectively.
In healthcare, information technology enables doctors to access medical records, diagnostic images, and specialist advice rapidly. In education, digital communication allows knowledge to cross geographical boundaries. In agriculture, farmers can receive weather, market, and crop information through mobile networks. In disaster management, early warnings communicated through digital platforms can save thousands of lives.
Artificial intelligence is now accelerating this transformation. It can analyze enormous amounts of information, identify patterns, and support decision-making within seconds. Recent reporting has even shown how AI can be exploited to collect information about military vessels, analyze satellite imagery, and conduct influence operations.
This creates both opportunity and danger.
The same technology that can save lives can also spread misinformation. The same communication network that connects families can be used for propaganda, manipulation, and cyberattacks. The same artificial intelligence that helps doctors can potentially assist criminals or hostile actors.
Therefore, technological power without ethical responsibility can become dangerous.
For developing countries such as Bangladesh, this global transformation offers an enormous opportunity. Bangladesh should not view information technology merely as a tool for social media or outsourcing. It should be treated as a national strategic asset.
The country needs stronger investment in cybersecurity, satellite technology, digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence, data science, and advanced communication systems.
Bangladesh needs a culture of intelligent communication. Political disagreement, business disputes, diplomatic tensions and social conflicts cannot always be solved through confrontation. Sometimes the most powerful weapon is a well-timed conversation.
The world is entering an era in which information moves at the speed of light, technology converts information into power, and communication determines how that power is used.
The Iran war has shown that knowing the battlefield can be as important as controlling it. Ukraine has demonstrated the strategic importance of secure communication. Contemporary diplomacy has shown that even after missiles are launched, communication remains the pathway toward de-escalation.
The lesson for the 21st century is therefore simple but profound: Weapons may win battles, but information shapes the battlefield -- and communication can determine whether the next battle happens at all.
For nations, institutions and individuals alike, the future will belong not simply to those who possess the most technology, but to those who can collect information intelligently, understand it accurately, and communicate it wisely.
Md Sultan Uddin is a banker.

item.title: Ensuring exports stay on the up. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh’s export performance in the first quarter of FY27 offers a welcome sign of resilience, especially at a time when the economy continues to face a range of challenges.
According to reports, merchandise exports rose by 6.34% year-on-year to $13.09 billion between July and September, while September alone recorded an 8.54% growth.
The continued strength of the readymade garment sector is also particularly encouraging. RMG exports grew 6.10% during the quarter to $10.58b, with both knitwear and woven garments recording solid growth.
This remains an important source of foreign exchange and employment, and its performance demonstrates the continued competitiveness of Bangladeshi exporters in global markets.
More encouraging still is the performance of several non-RMG sectors. Pharmaceutical exports grew 40.39%, while jute and jute goods rose 31.55%, leather and leather products 14.74%, and light engineering 16.51%.
These figures are proof that Bangladesh has considerable potential beyond its traditional dependence on garments.
However, this progress should be treated as an opportunity to build on rather than a reason for complacency. Agricultural products and frozen and live fish recorded negative growth, showing that important areas of the export basket still require attention.
Greater diversification will be essential if Bangladesh is to make its export earnings more resilient to changes in global demand.
The government must therefore focus on removing the structural obstacles that continue to affect exporters, including energy shortages, high production costs, logistical bottlenecks, and bureaucratic delays.
Support for product upgrading, market expansion, and trade facilitation must translate into practical measures that businesses can actually benefit from.
The latest figures are undoubtedly positive: They reflect the efforts of exporters and workers and the continued demand for Bangladeshi products.
Now, the priority should be to sustain this momentum, strengthen emerging sectors, and open more markets so that export growth becomes broader, more stable, and capable of supporting Bangladesh’s long-term economic ambitions.

item.title: Small businesses need more support. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The newly announced requirement making a Business Identification Number (BIN) mandatory for opening or operating business bank accounts and accessing loans has created serious difficulties for micro, small, and medium enterprises (CMSMEs).
While the objective of widening the tax and VAT net is understandable, its implementation must not undermine the very businesses that generate employment and drive economic activity.
Bangladesh needs more businesses to enter the formal economy, but this cannot happen if the process of becoming formal itself becomes a barrier to doing business.
Bangladesh has around 11.7 million economic units, nearly 99% of which are CMSMEs. Together, they employ more than 30 million people and contribute an estimated 25-32% of GDP. These businesses therefore cannot be treated as an administrative afterthought.
When entrepreneurs struggle to obtain the necessary documentation for a BIN, and consequently face delays in opening accounts or securing credit, the effects extend well beyond individual businesses.
The Association of Bankers, Bangladesh has already urged the National Board of Revenue to exempt micro, cottage, and small businesses or introduce a phased approach. The NBR, however, has said the requirement is mandated by law and cannot simply be waived.
This is precisely why the focus should now be on making compliance easier. If formalization is the goal, registration procedures should be simplified, documentation requirements reduced, services made genuinely accessible online, and adequate transition time provided.
Banks and relevant agencies should also coordinate so that entrepreneurs are not forced to navigate multiple layers of bureaucracy.
While revenue mobilization is important, creating an environment in which businesses can start, survive, and expand is equally necessary. Bangladesh needs more entrepreneurship, investment, and employment -- not more red tape.
The principle should be straightforward: Compliance must be encouraged, but doing business must be made easier. A stronger formal economy will only emerge from removing unnecessary obstacles instead of adding new ones.

item.title: Lahore ranked as the most polluted city in the world, again. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Lahore has once again emerged as the most polluted city in the world, with its air quality classified as “unhealthy”, according to air quality monitoring platform IQAir, as Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz said the government was making efforts to address environmental issues.

In the past few years, air pollution has become one of the most pressing public health and environmental crises facing Pakistan. Various cities of the country, most notably Lahore, deal with smog, especially in the winter months. The phenomenon is attributed mainly to industrial emissions, vehicular pollution, stubble burning and air movement.

Lahore topped the list of the most polluted cities on Friday morning, with an air quality index (AQI) of 167, according to the IQAir live tracker, falling under the ‘unhealthy’ category, closely followed by Bangladesh’s Dhaka at 164 and Egypt’s Cairo at 158.

Later in the day, Lahore’s ranking in the list of the world’s most polluted cities dropped to 10th, with an AQI of 149 at 2:00pm.

The provincial capital was the only Pakistani city ranking in the top 30 most polluted cities on Friday morning. The only other Pakistani city in the 125-city list was Karachi at 34th place with an AQI of 69, on Friday morning.

Later in the day, Karachi moved up a few spots to number 23 with an AQI of 75, as of 2:00pm.

According to IQAir, in Lahore, “PM2.5 concentration is currently 15.2 times the World Health Organisation annual PM2.5 guideline value”.

PM2.5 refers to fine inhalable particles, with diameters generally 2.5 micrometres and smaller. Of all air pollution measures, PM2.5 pollution poses the greatest health threat, according to IQAir.

According to the website, PM2.5 can enter the circulatory system and even the brain, causing serious health complications if long-term exposure occurs.

For those in Lahore, IQAir recommended avoiding outdoor exercise, closing windows to avoid outdoor air, wearing a mask outdoors and installing an air purifier indoors.

Meanwhile, in a televised address to senior officers in Lahore on Friday, Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz said the provincial government was making efforts to address environmental issues.

For the past eight years, she said, Lahore as well as some parts of Punjab would undergo a “smog shutdown” in September and October

“For three years now — I won’t say there is zero smog, but — there is less smog,” she said.

In January this year, Lahore was ranked as the most polluted city globally by IQAir with an AQI of 452. Earlier this week, a new analysis released by the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) ranked Lahore among cities whose ozone levels were “extremely poor”.

item.title: Towards stronger ties with Australia. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The recent diplomatic engagement with the Australian High Commission could help move our relationship beyond traditional development aid toward a more ambitious, economic-first alliance.
As Bangladesh navigates a critical economic transition, deepening ties with a nation such as Australia across energy security, trade diversification, and technical education is the sort of partnership that could help us with our ambitions for sustainable growth.
At the heart of this evolving relationship is the shared imperative of energy security. As Bangladesh works to power its industrial capacity and meet expanding domestic demand, securing reliable liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports and attracting foreign direct investment in renewable energy, energy exploration, and grid logistics are certainly essential.
Australia, with its vast energy resources, green technology leadership, and expertise in resource management, is a perfect fit to support our transition toward a more resilient and diversified energy matrix.
Equally promising is the focus on human capital development. Expanding pathways for skilled professional migration in engineering, healthcare, and information technology creates valuable opportunities for Bangladeshi talent while helping fill key labour demands in Australia.
Proposals to link Bangladesh’s technical training centres with Australian vocational institutions, alongside efforts to bring offshore university campuses to Dhaka, reflect forward-thinking vision for development. Aligning local skill training with international technical standards is the sort of initiative we need to see to ensure that our youth can learn to compete successfully in the global economy.
Strengthening Bangladesh-Australia cooperation in areas of mutual interest could be crucial for our ongoing economic transformation. This is a partnership that promises long-term stability and mutual prosperity, and we must ensure that we are ready to take this relationship to the next level.

item.title: Getting tougher on public accountability. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The forced resignation of a sitting lawmaker and the dissolution of local party committees following multiple land grabbing incidents and attempts potentially mark a critical turning point for political governance.
It goes without saying that when public representatives and grassroots operatives become implicated in acts of mob violence, land grabbing, and criminal sabotage, the integrity of the entire political system is compromised.
While organizational dismissals and parliamentary resignations are necessary first steps, and we commend the state for taking swift action, we must go far further to systematically excise bad actors from public life.
Political affiliation in Bangladesh has long functioned as a shield against legal accountability. Local leaders, clout-chasers, and organized muscle have routinely exploited political patronage to seize property, intimidate communities, and subvert laws with complete impunity.
Our law enforcement too is not above criticism; at a time when we have needed them to be proactive and assist with dismantling criminal activities, their passivity has only emboldened criminal behaviour.
What we have is a deep-seated culture of impunity that continues to undermine the rule of law, and it is one that we must eliminate.
Internal party discipline, while commendable, cannot replace state justice. Forcing rogue actors to step down or stripping them of party membership addresses the political optics, but it does not satisfy the demands of the law.
As such, criminal acts must be met with rigorous investigation, transparent prosecution, and severe judicial penalties, regardless of an individual's standing or political ties.
If our country is to break free from the destructive cycles of political hooliganism, we must expect better from our political leaders. The message must be clear: Extortionists and land grabbers have no place here.

item.title: Living longer, living better. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
On October 1, the world observes the International Day of Older Persons 2026 under the theme, "The Age of Longevity: Rethinking Systems for Longer Lives."
For Bangladesh, this theme arrives at a defining moment. We often celebrate our youthful workforce as the country's greatest demographic dividend, yet another profound demographic transformation is unfolding alongside it: Bangladesh is quietly becoming an ageing society.
Longer lives are one of humanity's greatest achievements. They reflect better healthcare, improved nutrition, and declining mortality.
But longevity also raises an important question: Are our institutions, transport systems, healthcare services and workplaces prepared for millions of citizens who will live well beyond 60?
An ageing Bangladesh
Bangladesh officially considers all citizens aged 60 years and above as senior citizens under the National Policy on Older Persons adopted in 2013.
According to the World Health Organization, Bangladesh now has approximately 16.5 million people aged 60 and above, representing around 10% of the national population.
By 2050, this share is projected to nearly double to 19%, meaning almost one in every five Bangladeshis will be an older person.
The transition is happening remarkably fast. Bangladesh moved from around 5% elderly population in 1990 to nearly 10% by 2024, and projections indicate that the country may become an "aged society" much earlier than many expected.
This transformation is occurring while Bangladesh still enjoys a relatively large working-age population. Rather than seeing youth and ageing as competing priorities, policy-makers should recognize them as two sides of the same demographic reality.
Living longer does not automatically mean living healthier. The WHO estimates show that after turning 60, Bangladeshi women can expect to live about 20.4 more years, while men can expect around 19 years.
However, several of those additional years are often spent coping with chronic illnesses, reduced mobility, and disability.
At the same time, traditional family structures are changing. Urbanization, overseas migration, and nuclear families are weakening the informal support systems that once cared for elderly parents.
Many grandparents now shoulder childcare responsibilities while their adult children work elsewhere. Longevity, therefore, is no longer merely a family issue. It has become a national policy issue.
What Bangladesh has already achieved
The country has not remained inactive. The Old Age Allowance program, introduced in 1997, now supports around 6.1 million beneficiaries, each receiving Tk 650 per month during FY2025-26, with a budget allocation of approximately Tk 4,791 crore. Payments are increasingly delivered through mobile financial services and agent banking, improving transparency.
The government has also launched the Universal Pension Scheme, aiming to build long-term retirement security for citizens aged 18 and above. The broader vision seeks to create a sustainable pension architecture before population ageing becomes overwhelming.
Additionally, the National Healthy Ageing Strategy and Action Plan (2024-2030) has begun laying the groundwork for more age-friendly healthcare services. These are important foundations, but they are only the beginning.
Time to build an age-friendly Bangladesh
The next phase requires rethinking everyday systems rather than creating isolated welfare programs.
First , make public transport truly elderly-friendly: Reserved seating exists on paper in many buses, but enforcement remains inconsistent.
Every metro rail coach, intercity train, launch and public bus should guarantee clearly marked priority seating, easy boarding facilities, handrails, ramps and audio-visual announcements designed for older passengers. Mobility is dignity.
Second , strengthen geriatric healthcare: Every district hospital should gradually establish dedicated geriatric care units. Community clinics can expand screening for hypertension, diabetes, dementia, osteoporosis, and vision problems among older citizens. Preventive care costs far less than crisis care.
Third, design age-friendly cities: Footpaths without obstacles, safer pedestrian crossings, benches in public spaces, accessible public toilets and well-lit walkways are not luxuries. They are essential infrastructure for an ageing society.
Fourth, modernize income security: The Old Age Allowance should gradually become more adequate and more inclusive, particularly for vulnerable elderly people living alone, widows and those with disabilities. The proposed multi-tier pension system -- combining tax-financed support, contributory pensions and voluntary savings -- deserves accelerated implementation.
The untapped resource called experience
Perhaps the greatest missed opportunity lies elsewhere. Bangladesh often measures productivity only through youth employment. Yet millions of retired teachers, agricultural experts, engineers, doctors, administrators, scientists, and skilled workers possess decades of institutional knowledge.
Instead of viewing retirement as the end of public contribution -- and rather than relying solely on ad hoc contractual appointments -- Bangladesh could establish a National Senior Expertise Pool, a structured national network of retired professionals from the civil service, agriculture, health, education, engineering and other technical sectors.
By harnessing their institutional memory, field experience and policy expertise, this pool could provide advisory support to government programs.
They would not replace serving officials or occupy promotional positions. Instead, they could serve as mentors, advisers, and technical resource persons, either voluntarily or with a modest honorarium.
Experienced retirees could mentor young entrepreneurs, advise local government projects, teach technical skills, support agricultural extension, assist disaster preparedness, and volunteer in schools and community organi z ations.
Such programs would also play a part to reduce loneliness while transferring invaluable knowledge across generations.
Countries facing ageing populations increasingly promote "active ageing" rather than passive retirement. Bangladesh can adopt the philosophy without enormous financial costs.
The country already acknowledges that retirement need not mean the end of public service. In recent years, several retired secretaries and senior officials have been reappointed on contractual terms to lead important ministries, reflecting the government's recognition that institutional memory and seasoned judgment can remain valuable beyond formal retirement.
Such a model would also promote intergenerational collaboration. Bangladesh's youthful workforce remains its greatest demographic strength, yet younger officers need opportunities to learn from those who have navigated complex administrative challenges before them.
The objective should not be to prolong careers indefinitely, but to preserve valuable knowledge that would otherwise disappear on the day of retirement.
Healthy longevity is not simply about adding years to life; it is about adding value to those years. When experienced citizens continue contributing to national development in meaningful ways, ageing becomes not a burden on society but one of its greatest untapped resources.
Md Refatul Hossain is former Additional Director, DAE, and Senior Consultant, Agonochain Limited. Email: refatdae87@gmail.com .
