item.title: Why true police reform remains Bangladesh’s unfinished revolution. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Viewing the Monsoon Revolution purely as a regime change, more than two years later, is a narrow, misconstrued perspective -- and a half-truth at best.
The popular uprising was never just about removing an increasingly authoritarian regime from power; its ambitions were far greater.
Rebuilding and reforming state institutions -- which had become inept, deeply corrupt and inefficient -- was the central underlying goal and subsequent focus of the 2024 July Revolution in Bangladesh.
What began as a student-led protest for merit-based public job quotas ultimately transformed into a sweeping national resistance against systemic corruption, authoritarianism, and the collapse of good governance and institutional accountability.
Once August 5 sealed the fate of the previous regime for the foreseeable future, an interim government finally held general elections, transferring power to the country's first elected government in nearly two decades.
This milestone ignited high aspirations that post-revolution Bangladesh’s dysfunctional, broken-down state institutions would finally be rebuilt to meet public expectations.
Unfortunately, that has not been the case.
The police force -- the backbone of the state’s law and order apparatus -- serves as a stark example. Over the past two years, spanning two successive administrations following the Awami League’s ouster, leadership across various tiers of the force has seen frequent shake-ups.
These changes have often appeared more politically-motivated than driven by professionalism. Furthermore, the period has been marked by a wave of forced and early retirements of high-ranking police officers.
For the broader population, these internal shuffles matter less than tangible results; the public simply desires a safer, more stable law and order situation, and a disciplined, professional police force that genuinely serves the people.
Unfortunately, recent developments -- such as lethal goons vandalizing public property late at night, sometimes within the immediate vicinity of police outposts -- clearly illustrate how rapidly public trust and institutional expectations are eroding.
Instead of a proactive police force, we are increasingly witnessing a reactive one, swinging into action and making sporadic arrests only after crimes have taken place in full public view.
The reason why a student-led protest demanding quota system reforms for government jobs so rapidly transformed into a nationwide uprising that culminated in a change of government was because the population harboured years of pent-up grievances over the collapse of state institutions, their persistent failure to deliver basic services, and unabated corruption.
While the quota system provided the initial spark and the regime change opened a window of opportunity, the underlying drivers of the movement were far more profound.
The July-August 2024 uprising, therefore, symbolized more than mere opposition to a specific system; it challenged the country’s entire development paradigm, which had long excluded the majority from its benefits while maintaining zero institutional accountability.
To re-establish this long-lost transparency, swift institutional reform should have been treated as the ultimate priority.
Unfortunately, much of the reform momentum gained during the Yunus-led transitional government has largely dissipated over the seven months following this year’s February elections.
Police reform is a stark example: the process has effectively stalled, slowing from high-stakes structural overhauls to cosmetic adjustments and deep institutional paralysis.
Following the July 2024 mass uprising -- where heavy-handed crackdowns resulted in the deaths of hundreds of protesters and sparked widespread public fury -- the interim government formed a dedicated Police Reform Commission in October 2024 to dismantle the force’s colonial-era command structure. However, the new parliament allowed the reform commission’s ordinance to lapse, creating a critical legislative vacuum.
Continuous changes of guard in the police hierarchy -- swapping leaders of one political inclination for another -- often offer a false promise of organizational revamp. Such superficial shuffling does little to instill genuine professionalism across the force.
When the public finds the police missing in times of emergency, replacing the faces of force commanders cannot restore eroded trust. Beyond superficial uniform alterations, forced retirements, and sweeping bureaucratic transfers, the force remains largely the shadow of its old self.
The new government, still in its first year in office, would render an invaluable service to the citizenry by completely dismantling this legacy of political weaponization.
The force must be brought under stringent public oversight and accountability. Only then can its members effectively serve the community, actively protecting citizens from everyday lawlessness, muggings, burglaries, and land grabs.
It is deeply troubling to see how a segment of grassroots politicians today stands accused of weaponizing young children and juveniles for so-called “gang” activities -- frequently under the very nose of law enforcement.
The tragic murder of a young boy, Apratim, in Comilla has laid bare critical allegations: That persistent police neglect in addressing prior offenses by these same perpetrators allowed local juvenile gangs to swell to such dangerous proportions.
Even more discouraging is the nature of the police response following Apratim’s death. The subsequent launch of sweeping, overnight drives has led to the wholesale detention of hundreds of young people. While such knee-jerk, high-handed sweeps might temporarily succeed in shifting the spotlight away from institutional negligence, they do nothing to mend a broken law and order ecosystem.
Criminalizing our youth en masse fails to address the root problem; it denies juveniles the healthy, supportive socio-political environment they desperately need to thrive away from a life of crime.
Wholesale drives and indiscriminate detentions of adolescents universally fail to contain juvenile gang activity over the long term. While mass sweeps provide a temporary visual deterrence that may briefly appease public anxiety following high-profile crimes, they act as little more than a bandage on a deeply systemic issue.
Because mass arrests frequently rely on physical appearance, location, or arbitrary gathering spots rather than specific evidence, they end up sweeping innocent adolescents alongside hardened ringleaders. This approach fosters deep resentment towards law enforcement and severely traumatizes minors who have committed no crimes.
Furthermore, when these youths are sent to overcrowded child development centres or regular judicial custody, they receive virtually no meaningful rehabilitation. Criminological studies consistently indicate that arrested juveniles frequently return to their neighbourhoods only to regroup, recruit new members, and change their gang names -- often becoming far more hardened by their time inside.
Crucially, juvenile gangs (locally known as kishor gangs ) do not operate in a vacuum. Instead, they are actively patronized by local political leaders and their criminal associates, who deploy these youths for territorial control, extortion, and political muscle.
Mass drives merely target expendable, underage foot soldiers while leaving the older, influential puppet masters entirely untouched.
Until the police force is fundamentally reformed, systemic corruption and inefficiencies will continue to lure officers into ignoring routine community policing and gang tracking, incentivizing them instead to conduct flashy mass detentions of minors while leaving politically linked adult handler networks unscathed.
The current BNP leadership and the government they administer must remain mindful of the harsh lessons a preceding BNP administration learned at a heavy cost in the early 2000s. Following the BNP’s assumption of office in late 2001, Bangladesh experienced a severe spike in violent crime, including rampant extortion, high-profile kidnappings, muggings, vigilante justice, and murders.
The response that followed -- a massive, joint military campaign known as “Operation Clean Heart” -- resulted in widespread human rights controversies that no modern, democratically-elected government should ever seek to emulate.
A reformed police force -- shielded from undue political influence and empowered to deliver public law and order professionally -- is the only sustainable deterrent against resorting to such heavy-handed military measures to tackle societal crime.
Reaz Ahmad is Editor, Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Diesel at Tk 135: How will it affect your food bill?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
In Bangladesh, whenever there is a hike in energy price, the consumers ask how much their food price is going to rise. The two are obviously related, but the amount that gets transferred from energy price to food price is not what it should be.
Diesel rose from Tk115 to Tk135 a litre on September 21, an increase of 17.4%. The recent price hike comes on the grounds that Bangladesh Petroleum Corporation’s loss has been mounting.
BPC lost Tk22,875 crore between March and August, and the budget FY 27 does not have any allocation to cover this loss. The Tk89,538 crore subsidy that the budget has provisioned for covers gas, electricity, and food.
BPC is recovering the loss by charging it to our pockets. But how much of the loss is it recovering? According to the government’s own formula, the market price for diesel should be Tk205 a litre. This means, at Tk135, we are still paying Tk70 less than what we should.
As such, the price hike only does a partial recovery of the loss for BPC -- about Tk10,000 crore of a Tk40,000 crore annual loss on diesel.
So was the price hike essential? Yes. Is it enough? No. Is there a risk of further price hike? Yes.
Then what would happen to the price of our food basket?
The evidence on how the rise in energy price transfers to food price in Bangladesh is scanty. Generally, the transfer is arbitrary and set by the traders.
We have results from April this year. The 15% adjustment then took food inflation from 8.39% in April to 9.06% in May, a gain of 0.67 percentage points in one month, before coming down to 7.02% by August. Non-food inflation rose and did not come back down.
In my reading, the current adjustment may add 0.7 to 1.2 percentage points to food inflation, with the peak in November or December.
However, that is the index. We need to measure what happens in the bazaars.
Let us look at one trader’s account from August 2022, after the largest rise in fuel price in our history. A Bogura trader moving fourteen tons to Dhaka increased his transport cost from Tk2 to Tk2.50 a kilogram. Freight is charged by weight, so that 50 poisha is what the lorry added to every kilogram of vegetable it carried, whatever the vegetable was.
In Dhaka, the price of okra went from Tk30 to Tk40 a kilo and long beans from Tk40 to Tk50. That 50 poisha of freight essentially translated to Tk10 a kilo for the consumer in Dhaka.
The Directorate of National Consumer Rights Protection did the same arithmetic on eggs three weeks later and published it. Their estimate showed that the fuel price rise had added four poisha to the cost of moving one egg. Traders put Tk2.70 on the price, and the wholesale margin went from under 20 poisha to Tk2.70 in four days.
Historically, fish prices have not moved with the price of diesel. Dhaka's tilapia, pangash, and rui prices were the same in the week before the September hike and the week after, while the price of ilish fell.
Farmed fish depends on electricity rather than on diesel. In June 2023, with no change in fuel price, koi, pangash, and tilapia rose Tk40 to Tk50 a kilo when ice plants could not freeze blocks during load shedding.
Ilish fishermen are heavily reliant on diesel as they go out for days at a time. But it is a buyer’s market and they cannot transfer the higher cost of diesel to the price of their catch. The traders dictate.
How about rice? The price transfer is not immediate. The rice on sale in Dhaka today was grown with diesel bought between January and early April, when the official price was Tk100 but farmers were paying Tk110 to Tk125 through the March shortage.
The Tk135 announced on September 21 enters the Boro crop planted this winter and harvested in April and May 2027. The transport cost immediately increased for rice when the cost of diesel was hiked. Four days after the hike, a sack cost Tk15 to Tk20 more at wholesale, and Paijam and Atash went from Tk56 to Tk60 a kilo at Mohammadpur.
From the analysis, we can reach some conclusions:
• The hike was necessary and it is not finished. A further adjustment is the base case, not a risk.
• Vegetables, rice, fish, eggs -- each carries the fuel cost through a different channel and on a different timetable, so a single pass-through figure is meaningless.
• The gap persists because nobody analyzes how the value chain works, so the price shifts to whoever can charge the most without challenge.
How do we solve these challenges?
Ensure that people know that traders cannot just arbitrarily raise prices when energy prices are hiked, and the only way they will know is if someone publishes the number. As most people are unaware of how price is set and transferred across the levels of the value chain, they accept whatever comes their way. The default assumption here is that the price is bound to rise.
The government should set a threshold for how much margin can be added at each stage of the chain and this should vary by commodity. The price transmission should follow the variability. A threshold on the margin is not a cap on the price.
Publish what each stage of the food chain adds, every month, as a standing official series. Price caps do not work and have never worked. The Philippines capped rice in September 2023 and the national average came in 16% above the ceiling. Hungary capped retail food prices for 17 months and recorded the highest food inflation in the European Union.
What has worked is publication of the margin. South Africa's Competition Commission publishes an essential food price monitor that sets the producer price against the retail price commodity by commodity.
Hungary, having failed with caps, switched in 2025 to a ceiling on the retail margin published alongside a public price monitor.
A cap hides the mark-up. A published margin forces the chain to pass costs in both directions. Bangladesh already collects the daily prices through the Department of Agricultural Marketing. What it does not publish is the spread.
Economies are always correcting themselves. That is not the failure. The failure is when we cannot ensure the conditions that allow the economy to be resilient in stormy weather and bullish when the sun is shining.
In Bangladesh, our economic governance runs on perforated umbrellas. When it rains, we get wet. When the sun comes out, we burn.
Md Rubaiyath Sarwar is Managing Director, Innovision Consulting.

item.title: There is no justice without funding. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The UNHCR’s warning that nearly 8.3 million refugees and other forcibly displaced people are at risk of losing vital assistance because of severe funding cuts should concern us all, and is yet another sign of justice only being spoken of but not translating into action.
This is particularly significant for Bangladesh and the Rohingya community within it. Nearly 1.2 million Rohingya refugees remain in Bangladesh, with conditions in Myanmar still unsuitable for safe, voluntary, and dignified repatriation. At the same time, humanitarian resources are shrinking.
This is a dangerous combination: Bangladesh has continued to host the Rohingya despite the enormous pressure the crisis places on its resources, local communities, and public services. Yet humanitarian assistance cannot be allowed to diminish simply because the crisis has lasted for years.
It must be understood that a prolonged crisis does not become a less serious one, and scaling back humanitarian agency assistance has real-life impacts on people who are already among the world’s most vulnerable.
UNHCR’s own figures underline the strain on the Bangladesh response: Its 2026 appeal for the Rohingya response was reduced to $710.5 million -- 26% below the previous year -- covering only the minimum required for lifesaving assistance.
There must, therefore, be greater international responsibility-sharing. Funding for food, healthcare, shelter, education and protection must be sustained, particularly for children and other vulnerable groups.
Aid cuts should not become another factor pushing desperate refugees towards dangerous coping mechanisms or irregular journeys.
At the same time, humanitarian funding cannot substitute for a political solution. The ultimate goal must remain safe, voluntary, dignified, and sustainable repatriation to Myanmar, and international pressure must continue to address the conditions that have made return impossible.
The UNHCR warning is a reminder that humanitarian crises do not disappear when attention moves elsewhere. For Bangladesh, the message is especially clear: The Rohingya cannot be forgotten, and neither can the international responsibility to help resolve their plight.

item.title: Being proactive to uphold communal harmony. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The government’s decision to begin early preparations for ensuring a peaceful and safe Durga Puja is a timely and necessary step.
With the festival fast approaching, early coordination among the relevant ministries, local administrations, and law enforcement agencies is important to ensure that celebrations across the country take place in a secure and festive environment.
It is even more encouraging to see that preparations have begun ahead of the celebrations rather than waiting for problems to emerge. The government has rightly emphasized vigilance at Puja mandaps, proper security during idol immersion, the prevention of rumours, and prompt legal action if any untoward incident occurs.
These measures are essential for protecting worshippers and ensuring that the festival can be observed without fear, disruption, or unnecessary hassle.
However, planning alone will not be enough. The real test will be whether these directives are properly followed through on the ground.
Local administrations and law enforcement agencies must remain alert throughout the celebrations -- particularly at crowded mandaps and during immersion.
Security arrangements should be practical and responsive, while traffic management and public services should be coordinated so that devotees and other residents can move around safely.
The emphasis on preventing rumours is equally important: Old or edited photographs and videos can quickly create tension, making timely verification and responsible communication essential.
At the same time, any incident that does occur must be investigated impartially, and those responsible must face the law. There should be no cover-ups, premature conclusions, or selective enforcement.
Durga Puja is a major religious and cultural occasion for Bangladesh’s Hindu community. Ensuring that it is celebrated peacefully is part of the state’s responsibility to protect citizens and uphold communal harmony.
These preparations are welcome. Now, the authorities must ensure that every measure announced is translated into effective action, so that people can celebrate freely, safely, and without unnecessary difficulties.

item.title: Rethinking public sector management and governance. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Effective public-sector management is fundamental to sustainable national development. Economic growth, social inclusion, environmental sustainability, and effective public service delivery ultimately depend upon the capacity of state institutions to formulate sound policies, manage public resources efficiently, enforce laws consistently, and maintain public trust.
Bangladesh has made substantial progress in economic and social development. However, sustaining and consolidating these achievements requires further strengthening of the institutional foundations of governance, including the rule of law, administrative accountability, civil service professionalism, merit-based human resource management, institutional integrity, and citizen-centred service delivery.
This series argues that weaknesses in public compliance should not be viewed solely as deficiencies in citizens’ civic consciousness. The effectiveness, consistency, and credibility of state institutions significantly influence citizens’ behaviour.
Where laws are consistently enforced and institutions operate predictably, citizens are more likely to comply. Conversely, selective or inconsistent enforcement can weaken public confidence and gradually normalise non-compliance.
My own experience in public administration over several decades has reinforced this observation.
In various capacities -- including assistant commissioner (land), magistrate, upazila nirbahi officer, deputy commissioner, senior official of different ministries, and managing director of a state-owned corporation -- I encountered situations in which professional and lawful decisions came into tension with the preferences of influential individuals.
On several occasions, I experienced pressure, threats, investigations, or transfers after declining to accommodate requests that, in my professional judgment, were inconsistent with applicable rules or the public interest.
These experiences strengthened my conviction that civil-service integrity cannot depend solely upon the personal courage of individual officers. It must be supported by institutional safeguards, transparent career-management systems, professional leadership, and accountability mechanisms that protect officials who act lawfully and in the public interest.
Bangladesh possesses a large pool of capable public servants recruited through competitive examinations. Yet recruitment alone is insufficient to create a high-performing public administration.
Continuous professional development, effective leadership, evidence-based career management, ethical standards, performance management, institutional incentives, and protection of professional integrity are equally important.
This series proposes the establishment of a human resources research cell (HRRC) within the Ministry of Public Administration. The proposed mechanism would undertake evidence-based research on civil-service workforce planning, competency development, career progression, leadership, organizational culture, performance management, integrity, and international best practices.
Ultimately, strengthening public-sector management is not simply an administrative reform agenda. It is an essential component of building state capacity, improving public service delivery, strengthening citizen trust, and achieving sustainable and inclusive national development.
Governance begins with the rule of law
“Country First” is a principle frequently invoked in public life. Its real significance, however, lies not in rhetoric but in whether public institutions and individuals consistently place the national and public interest above personal or sectional interests.
One of the most important manifestations of this principle is respect for the rule of law.
During official training abroad, I experienced a simple incident that provided an important lesson. On a holiday, three of us were returning to our destination after visiting a scenic location. We asked our vehicle driver to stop briefly beside a main road so that we could take a quick look around. He immediately declined.
When we asked why, he explained that parking on that section of the highway was prohibited by law. He regarded compliance not merely as a means of avoiding punishment but as an obligation to respect the laws of the state. He understood both the legal requirement and the consequences of non-compliance.
The incident raised an important governance question: Are citizens inherently unwilling to comply with laws, or does the effectiveness of public institutions shape citizens’ behaviour?
The experience suggested the latter.
A similar phenomenon can be observed in Bangladesh. In areas adjacent to cantonments, for example, drivers often demonstrate greater compliance with traffic regulations because enforcement is more visible and violations are more likely to result in immediate consequences.
As an assistant commissioner (land) at three different workplaces, I encountered several challenges in ensuring the lawful and transparent management of public resources. On one occasion, in an upazila, a superior authority sought to influence the disposal of trees that had fallen following a cyclone near a government office. There was pressure to dispose of the trees at a relatively low price.
I did not accommodate that pressure. Instead, I followed the prescribed procedure and arranged for the trees to be disposed of at a substantially higher value. The proceeds were deposited into the government treasury through the prescribed challan procedure.
Subsequently, an investigation was initiated against me following the intervention of the concerned authority. The investigation, however, found no wrongdoing on my part. On the contrary, the additional deputy commissioner (revenue) appreciated the manner in which I had performed my official responsibilities.
The experience reinforced a fundamental principle: An officer’s first responsibility is to the law and the public interest, rather than to the preferences of an individual superior.
This also illustrates a broader principle of governance. The credibility and consistency of state institutions influence public behaviour.
Accordingly, improving civic compliance requires more than awareness campaigns. It requires institutions capable of enforcing laws consistently, fairly, and predictably -- and public officials who can apply those laws without fear or favour.
State capacity and public-sector performance
Good governance depends upon state capacity -- the ability of public institutions to translate laws and policies into effective outcomes.
State capacity encompasses several interconnected dimensions:
A government may formulate sound policies, but their developmental impact will remain limited if implementing institutions lack adequate capacity.
My experience across field administration, the magistracy, ministries, development projects, and a state-owned corporation has demonstrated that institutional capacity depends not only upon formal structures but also upon the integrity and professionalism of the people operating those structures.
For this reason, public-sector reform should focus not only on creating new policies and institutions, but also on strengthening the organisational capabilities of existing institutions.
Political leadership and a professional civil service
In a democratic system, elected governments receive their mandate from citizens and establish political priorities. The civil service provides institutional continuity, technical expertise, policy advice, and implementation capacity.
These functions should be complementary.
A professional civil service should be responsive to the legitimate direction of the elected government while maintaining professional integrity, objectivity, and adherence to law.
Public servants are recruited through competitive examinations and are expected to develop specialized knowledge and professional competence throughout their careers. Their fundamental obligation should therefore be to the Constitution, the law, the state, and the citizens they serve -- not to individual political leaders or factions.
While serving in an upazila as assistant commissioner (land), I declined to implement what I regarded as an improper request from a divisional commissioner. Initially, I was threatened with adverse consequences, and subsequently, I was transferred to another workplace in circumstances that I perceived as punitive.
Similar experiences occurred at other stages of my career. While serving as a deputy commissioner, I declined to accommodate an irregular request from a state minister. Approximately a year later, I was transferred.
During my service in different ministries and while performing project-related responsibilities, I also encountered instances in which ministers, state ministers, and senior officials sought outcomes that, in my professional judgment, were inconsistent with established procedures.
These experiences did not lead me to conclude that political leadership and civil-service professionalism are inherently incompatible. Rather, they demonstrated the importance of establishing institutional boundaries within which political leadership can exercise legitimate democratic authority while professional officials can perform their statutory responsibilities without improper pressure.
The effectiveness of governance depends significantly on maintaining this appropriate relationship between democratic accountability and administrative professionalism.
Civil-service professionalism and institutional culture
During my career in public administration -- including field administration and service across different ministries and institutions -- I had opportunities through overseas training and professional engagements to observe administrative systems in other countries.
I found that effective public administrations generally place strong emphasis on professional dignity, transparency, competence, accountability, continuous learning, and public-service motivation.
Bangladesh also possesses a considerable pool of talented public servants. However, the effectiveness of a civil service cannot be determined solely by the quality of its recruitment process. The post-recruitment environment is equally important.
Formal training, in-service training, mentoring, leadership development, performance evaluation, ethical guidance, career planning, and organizational culture collectively determine whether individual talent is converted into institutional capability.
Where these systems are weak, public servants may experience excessive hierarchy, interpersonal or interdepartmental competition, inadequate intellectual development, limited transparency, risk aversion, and excessive dependence on informal networks.
These problems ultimately affect the performance of the state.
My own experience has shown that even an officer committed to professional integrity can become vulnerable when institutional safeguards are weak. Transfers, adverse administrative actions, or investigations can become instruments of pressure if personnel-management systems lack transparency and objective criteria.
Therefore, protecting civil-service professionalism requires more than exhorting individual officers to remain honest. The institutional environment must also make integrity professionally sustainable.
Meritocracy, integrity, and political neutrality
One of the most important principles of public-sector management is meritocracy.
Recruitment, promotion, posting, leadership selection, and professional development should be based primarily on competence, integrity, performance, and institutional need.
Political neutrality does not mean that the civil service should be unresponsive to an elected government. Rather, it means that public servants should implement lawful government decisions professionally without allowing partisan considerations to determine their professional conduct.
During my career, I served as a magistrate at different levels and participated in the adjudication of criminal cases. In performing judicial responsibilities, I sought to ensure that decisions were based on law and evidence, irrespective of external influence.
The experience reinforced my belief that public authority carries a corresponding responsibility. Whether an officer is exercising magisterial power, administering land, managing a district, implementing a development project, or managing a public corporation, the guiding principle should remain the same: Authority must be exercised in accordance with law and in the public interest.
Where political patronage becomes an important determinant of career progression, institutional incentives can become distorted. Officials may focus on cultivating relationships rather than improving professional competence and public-sector performance.
Such an environment can weaken institutional trust and undermine the long-term capacity of the state.
A professional civil servant should therefore not be measured by proximity to political power, display of authority, or accumulation of wealth. The appropriate measure is the quality, integrity, and public value of the service delivered.
Transparency and evidence-based career management
Transparency in public administration extends beyond financial disclosure or access to information. It should also encompass the processes through which public servants are evaluated, promoted, posted, disciplined, and assigned to strategic responsibilities.
Career decisions should be supported by objective evidence, including:
When an officer declines an improper request, there should be a clear distinction between legitimate administrative disagreement and punitive personnel action.
A transfer may sometimes be necessary for legitimate organisational reasons; however, personnel decisions should not become instruments for rewarding compliance with improper demands or punishing professional independence.
Institutional memory is particularly important during periods of administrative or political transition.
A professional public administration should avoid both rewarding officials merely because of political affiliation and penalizing competent officials because of perceived political association without objective evidence.
Personnel decisions should therefore be governed by transparent institutional processes rather than informal patronage.
This is essential for building a civil service that can maintain continuity and professionalism across successive governments.
Strategic human resource management
Modern public administration increasingly recognizes human resources as a strategic asset.
Governments invest substantially in infrastructure, technology, and physical institutions. Yet institutional performance ultimately depends upon the people operating those systems.
Strategic public-sector human-resource management should therefore address the complete employee lifecycle -- from recruitment to retirement.

Such an approach can help transform the civil service from a primarily personnel-administration system into a strategically managed professional workforce.
Professional integrity should also be treated as an organizational capability. An institution that recruits competent officers but does not protect them from improper pressure may ultimately lose the very capability it seeks to develop.
Establishing a human resources research cell

The HRRC could function as a specialised policy and research mechanism supporting long-term public-sector workforce reform.

item.title: When tolerance goes missing. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
In this part of the world, being a minority is rarely a completely comfortable experience. Across the Indian subcontinent, irrespective of the border one happens to live on, minorities live with a degree of unease that the majority can afford to ignore.
Sometimes it is vague apprehension, sometimes outright fear, and increasingly, a question of identity, dignity, and survival.
This is true of religious minorities, but also of linguistic, ethnic, and cultural ones. Intolerance towards minorities may well be the most corrosive malaise afflicting our societies today.
Durga Puja, the biggest festival of Bengali Hindus, is almost upon us in both Bengals. It should be a season of celebration, music, food, adda and, above all, an exuberant assertion of Bengali culture.
Instead, the festival arrives this year with an unmistakable whiff of anxiety.
In West Bengal, the new government has reportedly decreed that Durga Puja should not even be called " Sharadotsav ." Religious figures from the Hindi heartland are telling Bengalis what they should eat during their own festival, including suggestions that fish and meat ought to be kept away from the Puja table.
Hardline Hindutva organizations, meanwhile, are instructing Bengalis on how their Puja should be conducted, urging them to abandon the supposedly vulgar excesses of “theme pujas” and return to the purity of traditional ritual.
Bengalis, it appears, need lessons in how to be Bengali. One wonders what greater triumph of tolerance could possibly be demanded.
Look across the border and the picture is no less unsettling. I have no idea how many reports of vandalized Durga idols will emerge from different parts of Bangladesh this year. Nor do I know whether cricketers Litton Das or Soumya Sarkar will feel sufficiently secure to wish their fans on Durga Puja.
Will actor Yash Rohan once again proclaim his Hindu identity on social media, knowing what the trolls may throw at him? Will Chanchal Chowdhury again post a photograph of his mother wearing sindoor? I genuinely do not know.
And perhaps that is precisely what is so disturbing. A citizen should not have to calculate the risks before wishing others on a religious festival.
A film star should not have to wonder whether displaying his faith will make him a target. A cricketer should not have to decide whether a simple greeting could trigger a social-media storm. Yet here we are.
On this side of the border, there are other reminders of how selectively we apply the language of inconvenience. For generations, Kolkata's Red Road has hosted Eid prayers. This year, the practice was stopped on the grounds of civic inconvenience. Muslims, after some initial grumbling, accepted the decision.
Then came the curious part: The same road was closed for days for a Prime Minister's program. Apparently, some public inconveniences are more equal than others.
Across the border, the mother of a Hindu monk detained in a Bangladeshi jail lay on her deathbed. Yet the son was reportedly denied even the few hours of parole needed to see her one last time.
Indeed, over the past two years, Durga Puja itself has become an unlikely item on the India-Bangladesh diplomatic agenda. Delhi has repeatedly reminded Dhaka that the safety of minorities and peaceful celebration of Puja are the responsibility of the government in power.
Dhaka has responded with equal firmness: Minority protection is an internal matter, and India should first look at the treatment of Muslims in its own backyard.
Both governments have a point. Both governments also have a blind spot. The uncomfortable truth is that minorities on both sides of the border are vulnerable. And the larger social problem is not merely the occasional failure of the state. It is the steady erosion of tolerance within society itself.
History offers enough warnings. A nation state that cannot make its minorities feel secure eventually creates a problem much larger than minority rights. It weakens social cohesion, feeds grievance, damages internal security and, sooner or later, creates consequences beyond its own borders.
But history books are one thing. Electoral politics is another. In the brutal arithmetic of democracy, numbers matter.
A community that does not constitute a sufficiently large ‘voting block’ is unlikely to receive the same political attention as one that can determine electoral outcomes.
Governments may speak the language of constitutional equality, but political parties speak, more often than not, the language of numbers.
This is where the contradiction becomes particularly stark. Both India and Bangladesh have constitutional guarantees protecting fundamental rights. The freedom to practise one's religion, to live with dignity and security, and to preserve one's identity are not favours bestowed by a benevolent majority. They are rights.
The real question is what happens when constitutional rights encounter social prejudice and political expediency.
Bangladesh offers a particularly instructive example because its minority question is far more complicated than the familiar Hindu-Muslim binary.
After several visits to the country, I have come to realize that even within the category of “minority,” there are layers of vulnerability.
Bangladesh's Hindus, the country's largest religious minority, understandably occupy much of the public discussion. Their concerns are real, and the difficulties faced by sections of the Hindu community are well documented. But stop at Hindu identity and we miss the larger picture.
Consider the Urdu-speaking Bihari Muslims of Geneva Camp. They are Muslims in a predominantly Muslim country. Yet decades after the birth of Bangladesh, many remain socially and economically marginalized, struggling to be fully absorbed into the national mainstream. I have seen some of that unease myself.
Or take the Telugu-speaking Hindu scavengers of Dhaka's Methorpatti. Their story is different again. They told me that their families had traditionally performed this work for generations, going back to the British period. Now, they said, members of the Muslim majority were increasingly entering the same occupation.
And then there are the indigenous communities of the Chittagong Hill Tracts and the Garo Hills, minorities in an ethnic and cultural sense, whose conflicts with people from the plains over land, resources, and their right to preserve their way of life have continued for decades.
Different communities. Different histories. Different grievances. But beneath them runs the same uncomfortable thread: The majority's difficulty in accommodating difference.
The mirror image exists on this side of the border too. What I sometimes call “Greater Bengal,” stretching across West Bengal, Tripura, and Assam, has its own catalogue of minority anxieties.
In West Bengal, a government with an unmistakable religious identity has recently come to power. Sections of the majority community, emboldened by the new political climate, appear increasingly comfortable displaying their religious muscle.
The result is predictable: Minorities retreat. They become more guarded about their identity, withdraw into familiar neighbourhoods and communities, and the psychological walls of the ghetto grow higher.
Assam has spent the past decade living with the anxieties surrounding the NRC, citizenship, and delimitation. For ethnic and linguistic minorities, questions of belonging and political representation are not abstract constitutional debates. They touch everyday life.
Tripura presents another version of the same story. Indigenous tribal communities increasingly fear that the state is intruding into their traditional way of life and that the Bengali Hindu majority is gradually overwhelming their language, culture, and social space. Again, the fault line is different. Again, the underlying problem is remarkably similar. We have forgotten how to live with differences.
There is a larger South Asian lesson here. Good news travels slowly across borders. Bad news travels at extraordinary speed. A progressive reform in one country may take years to influence the other. But a communal riot, an attack on a temple or mosque, a provocative speech or a piece of hateful social-media propaganda can cross the border almost instantly. Hatred needs no visa.
That is why the treatment of minorities cannot be dismissed as an internal matter by either India or Bangladesh. The two countries may disagree on almost everything else, but they are tied together by geography, history, language, religion, culture, and memory. What happens to minorities in one country inevitably resonates among communities across the border.
So, as Durga Puja approaches, perhaps the real test is not how grandly we celebrate our own faith, but how comfortable we are allowing somebody else to celebrate theirs.
India and Bangladesh do not need more sermons on secularism. They need the less glamorous business of enforcing the rights already promised by their constitutions.
Governments must protect minorities even when doing so is electorally inconvenient. Political leaders must resist majoritarian pressure rather than ride it. And societies must learn, once again, that difference is not an existential threat.
A minority does not ask for special treatment. It asks not to be treated as a problem. That should not be too much to ask in either Bengal. Because if the state fails to protect its minorities, the consequences will not remain neatly confined within national borders.
Fear will travel. Grievance will travel. Retaliatory politics will travel. And eventually, so will the bill.
Dr Anindita Ghoshal is Professor of History at Presidency University, Kolkata. Views expressed are the writer’s own.

item.title: Bangladesh women lose ground after quota reform. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Bangladesh’s 2024 student-led uprising was fuelled by a demand that coveted government jobs be awarded on merit, not through quotas.

The movement succeeded, the government was overthrown, and the quota system was largely scrapped — but the reform has had unintended consequences.

Women are securing a shrinking share of public sector jobs in the Muslim-majority nation of 170 million people.

Tothapi Azad, a 25-year-old Dhaka University graduate, supported calls to end quotas — but says she should have supported retaining them for women.

“For me, who had my family’s support, a quota might not have been essential — but for an average woman, it was essential,” she told AFP.

“A job is a tool for women’s empowerment. For rural women, it is more than that — a survival tactic, a shield to resist domestic violence.”

Data shows that the share of female government recruits has fallen since quotas were cut, shrinking an already limited number of civil service roles held by women.

‘Uncomfortable’

Until 2018, quotas accounted for 56 per cent of Class I posts, the top ranking civil service and public sector jobs.

That included 10pc for women, as well as 30pc for descendants of those who fought for Bangladesh’s independence in 1971.

Another 16pc was reserved for underprivileged regions and people with disabilities.

In 2018, after student protests, the then prime minister Sheikh Hassina scrapped quotas.

In 2024, it was proposed to reinstate quotas, sparking student protests.

That escalated into a mass uprising, and Hasina was overthrown.

Today, 93pc are filled on merit. A 7pc quota is reserved for those related to freedom fighters and other smaller groups, and there is no quota for women.

The Bangladesh Public Service Commission (BPSC), which runs the recruitment examinations, has around 300,000 applicants each year for 2,500-3,000 Class I jobs.

Before the quota was scrapped in 2018, women accounted for up to 35pc of recruits, including both quota and merit-based appointments.

That has dropped to 19pc, according to figures from the last exam round.

A BPSC official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said the body “finds the outcome uncomfortable”, but that its “duty is limited to conducting the examination”.

AKM Abdul Awal Majumdar, a former bureaucrat, backs merit-based recruitment but advocates coaching to help women compete.

“My female colleagues were unparallelled,” he said.

The government elected in February also backs merit-based recruitment.

Md Abdul Bari, a public administration minister, described it as a “rational reform” in parliament.

But some officials fear the decline in female recruitment will become increasingly visible.

“At this moment, at least 21 women are leading 21 districts,” said a female bureaucrat with 20 years of experience, speaking on condition of anonymity.

“In 10 years’ time, there won’t be this many women in the service.”

‘Can’t continue’

The impact goes beyond the civil service.

Police data shows that only 267 women out of 2,651 candidates qualified as constables this year.

Only six of the 184 candidates who qualified as police sub-inspectors were women. No women qualified as sergeants, compared with 96 men.

“We can’t continue without them,” a police officer told AFP, noting that every station has dedicated desks for women and children.

Bangladesh previously had 60pc quotas for women in primary teaching positions. That has also ended.

Asif Shahan, a Dhaka University professor of Development Studies, said fewer women in government would impact policymaking.

“Their issues get reflected in policy,” he told AFP.

The debate has split students.

Md Mazharul Islam, a Dhaka University students’ union career advisor, a supporter of the Islamist party Jamaat-e-Islami, backs a merit system.

“Society was much more conservative before, and girls were not allowed to pursue higher education,” he said.

“That has changed.”

Philosophy student Adity Islam said abolishing the women’s quota was wrong.

“We measured women across all walks of life with the yardstick of female students at Dhaka University,” said Islam, who is involved in leftist politics.

“Cutting the quota for women would eventually impact the overall governance system. We have already seen that in some districts. So aspiring candidates in many other places will lose hope.”

item.title: Zero tolerance for organized land grabs. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The alarming wave of violence pertaining to land grabs sweeping across Dhaka over recent days marks a dangerous collapse of civil order that must be met with uncompromising force from our authorities concerned.
That within three days, four separate properties across the capital -- Radda clinic in Mirpur, a housing compound in Mohammadpur, a residential building in Adabor, and a creative studio at ECB Chattar -- were targeted by organized, armed mobs shows just how dire the state of law and order is currently in the country.
How is it that hundreds of hired goons, wielding guns, machetes, and heavy machinery, can arrive in trucks to intimidate residents, vandalize structures, and seize land? This is no longer merely a series of civil property disputes but brazen gang violence, and it must end immediately.
Whatever political realignments have taken place since August 2024, the fundamental premise of a law-governed society remains unchanged: Legal ownership and possession must be determined exclusively through the judiciary and not through mob mobilization. This should not be a complex matter to grasp.
We must once again question our law enforcement agencies and their utter failure in preventing attacks of such massive scale. While recent arrests and stern promises from top police officials are at least a step in the right direction, words alone will not reassure a terrified citizenry.
We need the state to institute an absolute, zero-tolerance policy against organized land grabbing. Law enforcement must hunt down, arrest, and prosecute not only the hired foot soldiers, but crucially the ones calling the shots and orchestrating these operations.
There is simply no room for error on the part of our law enforcement, who must become more effective, not just at apprehending these criminals but also gathering intelligence to prevent such attacks.
If the state fails to crush this emerging apparatus of mob intimidation with unyielding resolve, it surrenders the capital to anarchy, and undermines any development ambitions we have. We cannot allow that to happen.

item.title: A child’s innocence and a world of cruelty. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
There are images that travel through social media because they are extraordinary. Then there are images that travel because they reveal something painfully ordinary about us.
The video from Uzirpur, Barishal, belongs to the second category. A little girl sits beside her father, who is tied to a roadside pole after being accused of theft. She dips pieces of bread into tea and feeds him with her own hands. Around them, people watch. Someone records. Later, thousands of people watch the recording.
The image is heartbreaking, but perhaps we should resist the temptation to stop at heartbreak.
The child has become the emotional centre of the story, but the real question is not simply why she fed her father. The more uncomfortable question is why her father was left tied to a pole in the first place.
According to reports, the man was detained by local people in Bamrail Bazar, Uzirpur, late on September 25 over an alleged attempt to steal. He was reportedly beaten and tied to a pole overnight. Police were informed but arrived after he had already been released by locals. No formal complaint was filed at the time.
Later, the upazila administration became involved, and officials arranged for the man to be taken to a rehabilitation centre following allegations of drug use. The administration also said it would support the child's education and help her mother find employment. The theft allegation itself remains a matter of conflicting accounts and has not been established through a judicial process.
That distinction matters. A person may be guilty of theft. He may have a history of offending. He may struggle with addiction. None of these possibilities gives a crowd the authority to become judge, jury, and jailer.
This is where the incident becomes larger than one accused man in one market. It forces us to ask what happens when the machinery of justice is replaced by the impatience of the crowd.
We often speak about the rule of law as though it were an abstract constitutional principle. In reality, the rule of law begins with something much more basic: A person accused of a crime remains a person.
The French novelist Victor Hugo understood this moral complication remarkably well. In Les Misérables , Jean Valjean's theft of bread is not presented simply as a question of whether stealing is right or wrong. Hugo asks us to look at the social world that surrounds the act.
The crime matters, but so does the hunger, exclusion, and desperation that make the crime intelligible. Understanding an offense does not mean excusing it. It means refusing to reduce a human being to the worst thing he may have done.
That distinction seems particularly relevant here. If the allegations against the man are true, he should face the consequences established by law. If he is struggling with addiction, he needs treatment. If poverty or family circumstances contributed to his situation, society should address those conditions.
None of these responses requires compassion to replace accountability. Rather, genuine accountability requires a system capable of distinguishing punishment from humiliation.
What happened in Uzirpur appears to have done the opposite. Before the facts were established, punishment came first. The rope came before the verdict.
There is another unsettling element in the video. The crowd did not merely restrain a man. His humiliation became public theatre. People gathered around him. Some reportedly demanded harsher treatment. A passerby recorded the scene and uploaded it to Facebook.
The video then travelled far beyond the market. The same technology that allowed the public to witness the injustice also transformed a child's distress into a piece of viral content.
This is one of the darker contradictions of the social media age. We are increasingly able to see suffering, but seeing suffering does not necessarily make us more humane. Sometimes it simply makes us spectators.
Hannah Arendt's writings on the relationship between ordinary people and systems of wrongdoing offer a useful philosophical lens here. Great harm does not always require extraordinary villains. Sometimes it emerges through ordinary people surrendering moral responsibility to the crowd, the institution or the situation.
The frightening question is not whether every person present intended cruelty but whether anyone stopped to ask the simplest question: What gives us the right to do this?
And then came the child.
She did not investigate the theft allegation. She did not ask whether her father was innocent. She did not know the procedural language of justice. She simply saw a hungry and humiliated human being whom she knew as her father. Her response was not a legal argument. It was an act of recognition.
Perhaps that is why the image unsettled so many people. The adults around the pole were looking at an accused thief. The child was looking at her father.
There is something profoundly important in that difference.
Modern societies build institutions precisely because human emotions are unreliable. Anger demands immediate punishment. Fear demands protection. Revenge demands spectacle.
Law is supposed to slow these impulses down. It asks us to investigate, establish facts, hear both sides, and impose proportionate consequences. In that sense, due process is not a luxury for respectable people. It is a protection for everyone, including those we dislike.
Immanuel Kant argued that human beings should never be treated merely as means to an end. The principle is particularly powerful here. A person accused of theft cannot become an object through which a crowd demonstrates its anger or moral superiority. Nor should a child's emotional suffering become entertainment for thousands of viewers.
The most encouraging part of this story came after the video spread. The administration intervened, arranged rehabilitation for the father, and promised support for the child's education and her mother's livelihood.
These steps are important because they recognize that punishment alone cannot solve problems involving addiction, poverty, and family vulnerability.
But institutional intervention should not depend on virality.
That may be the most important lesson from the incident. What if nobody had recorded the video? What if the child had not been there? What if the image had not touched the emotions of millions? Would the man still have been released? Would anyone have asked about his family? Would anyone have considered the child's education?
A society in which compassion arrives only after a video goes viral is a society that has outsourced conscience to the algorithm.
We should also be careful about romanticizing the father-daughter scene. It is tempting to say that the video proves that the man is a good father despite everything else. We do not know enough to make such a conclusion.
A single tender moment cannot erase allegations or family difficulties. Nor should the child's love be used to excuse any wrongdoing. Children can love people whose actions are deeply flawed. That is precisely what makes childhood both beautiful and vulnerable.
The little girl did not prove her father's innocence. She revealed our responsibility. Her small hands holding bread may have done something that the adults around the pole failed to do. They restored his humanity.
Perhaps that is why we should remember the image differently. Not as a sentimental story about a loving daughter, and not as evidence that an accused man was either good or bad. We should remember it as a question placed before an entire community.
When someone is accused of a crime, do we want justice, or do we simply want someone to suffer?
The difference between those two desires is the difference between a society governed by law and one governed by the crowd.
And sometimes, astonishingly, it takes a child with a piece of bread dipped in tea to remind the adults of that difference.
HM Nazmul Alam is an academic, journalist, and political analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently he teaches at IUBAT. He can be reached at nazmulalam.rijohn@gmail.com .

item.title: Unlocking our tourism potential. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
It would not be an exaggeration to say that, among the sectors in our country that have yet to scratch the surface regarding their true potential, tourism is among the most significant.
Bangladesh possesses all the ingredients of a world-class travel destination. From the world’s longest natural sea beach at Cox’s Bazar and the dense, mangrove ecosystems of the Sundarbans to the tea gardens, hills, forests, haors, waterfalls and lakes of Moulvibazar and Sreemangal, our natural diversity is undeniable.
Yet, despite this immense wealth of potential, Bangladesh’s tourism sector continues to flounder under the weight of neglected infrastructure, bureaucratic apathy, and a glaring lack of integrated national planning.
Across the country, the tourist experience remains severely hindered by basic administrative failures. Key destinations routinely lack fundamental amenities like clean public sanitation, safe drinking water, reliable transportation, clear signage, and functioning information centres.
Unregulated visitor surges during peak seasons result in severe traffic bottlenecks, while unmanaged plastic waste threatens fragile ecological reserves. Furthermore, the absence of streamlined visa processes, poor international marketing, and inadequate last-mile connectivity keep foreign tourists at bay, leaving the sector almost entirely reliant on a domestic market that receives little structural support.
To unlock the economic power of tourism, the government must move past piecemeal interventions and institute a coordinated, national tourism framework.
This requires developing community-based eco-tourism initiatives, enforcing strict environmental regulations in ecologically sensitive areas, and investing in specialized hospitality training.
Global tourism is a multi-billion-dollar driver of employment, foreign exchange, and regional economic development. Our administration must treat the industry not as an accidental byproduct of economic activity, but as a strategic national priority.
With proper investment, transparent governance, and a clear vision, we must look to transform our tourism sector into a sustainable pillar of national prosperity.vvvvv
